figure_analogy: two figures related by a rule, then a third with options; pick the figure completing the analogy (ICAR figural analogies)
figure_analogy: simple A:B::C:? with one clear change (e.g. big to small)
figure_analogy: A:B::C:? with two shapes changing by one combined rule (size and shade)
one_liner: A first shape turns into a second; the child makes the third shape change the same way by picking the matching fourth.
interaction: The top row shows A with an animated morph arrow into B. The bottom row shows C, an arrow, and an empty slot with 4 options below. The child taps the option that is to C what B is to A; it snaps into the slot. An optional two-icon confidence tap (a star for sure, a wavy hand for not sure) appears, then GO submits.
self_teach: The ghost-hand replays the A-to-B morph (e.g., big shrinks to small), then applies the same shrink to C and taps the matching option; the analogy row lights up. Warm-up: big circle to small circle, so big square to ? (small square).

learning_science.why: Analogical reasoning requires mapping the relation, not the surface, from base to target.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors include a literal copy of C and a wrong-transform foil so only relational mapping, not surface matching, is credited.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), Cognitive Science 7(2)

learning_science.why: Children move from surface to relational responding as knowledge and working memory grow, setting a floor age for abstract figural analogy.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Bands start at grades 2-3 with a single obvious change and add a second combined rule by 6-8, matching the relational shift.
learning_science.source: Rattermann & Gentner (1998), in Piaget, Evolution, and Development

learning_science.why: Confidence accuracy adds incremental validity and down-weights lucky guesses at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A quick optional two-level confidence tap is collected on a subset so calibration can be modeled without burden.
learning_science.source: Fleming & Lau (2014), Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 8:443

tail_precision_rationale: M-ERRTYPE uses a designed distractor set - a literal-copy foil (no transform applied), a wrong-attribute foil, and an over/under-application foil - so a wrong answer reveals exactly where the relational mapping broke and grades how far below the analogy cut a child sits. On two-rule items the same distractor keying feeds the proposed M-RULEID (how many transformations were correctly applied), separating one-rule from two-rule mappers at the tail. M-RTFIRST captures the map-before-act latency typical of strong reasoners, and M-CONF on a subset removes lucky guesses via confidence-accuracy calibration.
age_rationale: Figural analogy requires holding an abstract transformation and re-applying it. With familiar relations this appears early, but reliable mapping over arbitrary figural transforms is not dependable until roughly grades 2-3 (ages 7-9); K-1 is excluded because at ages 5-6 such mapping is unstable and would measure developmental stage rather than reasoning (Goswami 1992; Rattermann & Gentner 1998). 2-3 uses one salient change; 4-5 a clear single transform with confusable foils; 6-8 combines two transforms. Big tap options keep motor demands low.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious transform A:B::C:? (grades 2-3) up to two combined transforms with relational distractors (6-8)
difficulty_levers: transformation type: size, rotation, fill/shade, count, reflection, add/delete element
distractor design: literal-copy, wrong-attribute, over-application foils
adaptive.notes: A:B::C:? items generate from a transform grammar with relationally-keyed distractors; unlimited clones and clean difficulty control via transform count.

engagement_hook: A magic morph - watching A visibly transform into B and then casting the same spell on C is playful and makes the hidden rule tangible.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Exclude K-1 to avoid measuring the relational shift instead of reasoning; include a literal-copy foil so surface matching does not score; pair shade/color with shape; keep the confidence tap optional and non-punitive; big tap options remove motor load; the ghost-hand morph plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Sorting Gate
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: two sets of six figures; the left satisfy a hidden rule and the right violate it - discover the rule that distinguishes the sets
visual_rule_discovery: two labeled bins each show a few example figures; place new figures into the bin whose secret rule they match
one_liner: Two bins each show example figures; the child drops each new figure into the bin whose secret rule it matches.
interaction: Two bins (shown by icon, not words) each display 3-4 example figures obeying a hidden rule (e.g., left = has a hole, right = solid). New figures appear one at a time; the child drags each into a bin (or taps the figure then taps a bin) and gets an immediate settle/glow. After a fixed number of figures the child taps GO to score the final placements. A hint lamp can be tapped to reveal one extra worked example.
self_teach: The ghost-hand picks the first queued figure, hovers it over the left bin then the right bin (weighing it), then drops it into the correct bin, which accepts with a glow while the wrong bin gives a soft nudge back. Warm-up uses an obvious color rule (red bin, blue bin).

learning_science.principle: Concept attainment / rule discovery by hypothesis testing
learning_science.why: Inducing a category boundary from positive and negative examples is prototypical inductive reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must infer the hidden rule from exemplars and test it by placement, with feedback enabling hypothesis revision.
learning_science.source: Bruner, Goodnow & Austin (1956), A Study of Thinking

learning_science.principle: Feedback that informs the next action
learning_science.why: Immediate task-level feedback drives the fastest correct rule revision.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each placement gives instant accept/nudge feedback so the child can update the hypothesis on the very next figure.
learning_science.source: Hattie & Timperley (2007), Review of Educational Research 77(1)

learning_science.why: Gameplay actions can be logged as evidence of competency without stopping to test.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The placement stream is logged as evidence of rule induction (accuracy trajectory, test informativeness), not only a final score.
learning_science.source: Shute (2011), in Computer Games and Instruction

new_measurements_proposed.name: Hypothesis-search efficiency
new_measurements_proposed.what: Informativeness of the child's exploratory choices during rule discovery: how quickly errors are eliminated and whether placements test maximally disambiguating cases versus redundant or random ones.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: In rule-discovery tasks, able children run efficient disambiguating tests and converge fast; this indexes inductive/scientific reasoning and dynamic-assessment learning rate, adding tail signal beyond final accuracy and resisting coaching.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: From the placement/action log, compute the reduction in the viable-rule space per action (or trials-to-criterion after the first informative feedback) and flag perseverative or random tests.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=1 rule-discovery item with >=6 feedback-bearing actions; aggregate over >=3 such items for a stable rate.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PROG turns one puzzle into a rule-acquisition curve: running accuracy across placements shows how fast the child locks the hidden rule (trials-to-criterion), a dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal with tail validity beyond a static score. The proposed M-HYP scores how disambiguating each placement is (does the child test the informative ambiguous cases or only obvious ones), isolating strategic inductive reasoners at the ceiling. M-HINT (hint-free discovery is stronger evidence) and M-EXPLORE round out a process picture a single accuracy bit cannot give.
age_rationale: Rule discovery from examples requires generating and revising hypotheses, which is unreliable in K-1; the youngest band is served by the five simpler FLU types instead. 2-3 uses a single-feature hidden rule with feedback; 4-5 uses less salient single features; 6-8 uses conjunctive or relational hidden rules with no feedback until GO. Drag or tap-to-bin with large targets keeps motor demands modest.

adaptive.content_range: single obvious-feature sort with feedback (grades 2-3) up to conjunctive/relational hidden rules with delayed feedback (6-8)
difficulty_levers: rule complexity: single feature to conjunction to relational/relational-count
number of worked examples before testing
feedback immediate vs delayed to GO
adaptive.notes: Rules and exemplar sets are procedurally sampled but require an audit that the exemplars uniquely identify the intended rule, so cloning is high-throughput with a uniqueness check.

engagement_hook: Cracking a secret sorting rule - each correct drop confirms your theory with a glow, and the aha of guessing the rule is intrinsically rewarding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Audit that exemplars determine a unique rule so M-HYP and M-PROG are meaningful; pair color with shape/pattern; large bins and snap placement reduce motor load; keep hints non-punitive but logged; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 to avoid floor effects that would misread as low ability.

name: Copy the Change
topics_techniques_covered: visual_rule_discovery: a few input-to-output grid examples demonstrate a transformation rule; infer the rule and construct the output grid for a new input
visual_rule_discovery: one worked example shows a small grid changing (e.g. all shapes shift right); apply the same change to a new grid by tapping cells
one_liner: A small example shows a grid changing; the child makes the same change happen on a new grid by tapping cells.
interaction: The top shows a worked example as an animated before-to-after grid pair. Below sit a new before grid and an editable after grid (initialized as a copy of the new before). The child taps cells to change them (a tap cycles a cell through the available colors/states; tap-and-hold clears) to produce the transformed output, then taps GO. Snap-to-cell tapping; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand plays the example transform (e.g., every filled cell slides one column right) as an animation, then on the new grid taps the cells to reproduce the same slide; the output glows when it matches. Warm-up: a one-row 1x3 shift.

learning_science.principle: Abstraction and reasoning from few examples
learning_science.why: Inferring a transformation from one or few input-output pairs and applying it to a new case is a hallmark of fluid intelligence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items give one or few worked transforms and require constructing (not selecting) the output, following the ARC abstraction-and-reasoning paradigm.
learning_science.source: Chollet (2019), On the Measure of Intelligence, arXiv:1911.01547

learning_science.why: A studied example plus a completion problem builds a transferable schema at lower load than open problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child studies the animated example, then completes the analogous output - a completion-problem design.
learning_science.source: Renkl & Atkinson (2003), Educational Psychologist 38(1)

learning_science.why: Building an output rather than picking one yields per-cell graded evidence and blocks lucky guessing.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The output is scored per cell (polytomous) so near-correct constructions earn graded credit.
learning_science.source: Embretson & Reise (2000), Item Response Theory for Psychologists

tail_precision_rationale: Because the child constructs the output, M-POLY scores per-cell correctness so a near-correct grid (right rule, one slip) earns graded credit and places the child precisely where free selection cannot. M-PATH with M-EFF compare the child's edit sequence to the minimal set of changes: constructing exactly the needed cells (no flailing) at a multi-rule transform is a strong ceiling separator and feeds the proposed M-HYP for how systematically the rule was applied. M-REV and M-PROG show whether the child locked the rule immediately or converged by trial-and-error. Guessing is near-impossible for a constructed grid, so accuracy at high difficulty is unusually clean tail evidence.
age_rationale: Constructing a transformed grid demands inferring a rule and executing multiple coordinated edits, exceeding K-1 fine-motor control and working memory; K-1 is covered by the simpler selection-based FLU types. 2-3 applies a single shown transform (shift/recolor) on a small grid; 4-5 infers the transform from one example; 6-8 infers multi-step or conditional transforms on larger grids. Tap-to-cycle cells with large targets keep edits feasible from grade 2 up.

adaptive.content_range: apply a single shown transform on a small grid (grades 2-3) up to infer-and-construct multi-step or conditional transforms on larger grids (6-8, ARC-like tail)
difficulty_levers: transformation complexity: translate to recolor to reflect/rotate to conditional/relational
grid size and number of objects
one worked example vs infer from multiple examples
whether the examples imply a single vs multiple plausible rules
adaptive.notes: Transforms are program-sampled and applied to random grids to make input-output pairs; needs a check that the shown examples imply a unique transform, so cloning is high-throughput with a uniqueness audit.

engagement_hook: You are the copy-machine wizard - learn a secret change from one example then perform it yourself; building the answer feels like casting the rule rather than picking from a menu.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Ensure the example(s) imply a unique transform so per-cell scoring is fair; large tap-to-cycle cells plus undo reduce motor and slip errors; pair color with pattern; no reading; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; exclude K-1 due to multi-edit motor and working-memory demands.

name: Twin Tap
topics_techniques_covered: visual_matching: tap same (smiley) / different (frowny) on two side-by-side patterns as fast as possible
visual_matching: same/not-same when figures differ by one feature (color or an added dot)
visual_matching: identical-or-different judgement on 3/6/9-digit number strings
visual_matching: one-versus-many same/different for older children
one_liner: Two cards flash side by side and the child slams SAME or DIFFERENT as fast as they can while staying correct.
interaction: Two stimuli render simultaneously; the child taps one of two large fixed buttons — a smiley SAME (left) or frowny DIFFERENT (right). The tap submits immediately; the next pair appears after brief feedback. No typing, no scrolling.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows two identical shapes then a hand tapping the smiley (which glows), then two different shapes and the hand tapping the frowny. One unscored warm-up pair with green/red feedback runs before any scored trial.

learning_science.why: Under time pressure children can trade accuracy for speed, so uncontrolled scoring rewards impulsive fast-wrong responding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: RT is credited only on correct trials and the combo breaks on any error, so speed counts only when accuracy is held (M-SPEEDACC).
learning_science.source: Wickelgren, W. A. (1977). Speed-accuracy tradeoff and information processing dynamics. Acta Psychologica, 41(1), 67-85.

learning_science.why: A child's slowest responses correlate with ability more strongly than their fastest, so consistency beats peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Report RT variability (CV) and slow-tail lapse frequency (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) rather than best or mean RT.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A 'worst performance' analysis of individual differences. Intelligence, 14(3), 309-325.

learning_science.why: A novel speeded mechanic must be understood without reading to avoid construct-irrelevant novelty variance.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand demo plus one unscored warm-up trial teach the SAME/DIFFERENT mapping before scoring begins.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59-89.

tail_precision_rationale: Raw same/different speed barely separates the gifted tail, so tail precision comes indirectly: (a) intra-individual consistency - low RT variability and few slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) track ability better than peak speed (worst-performance rule); (b) an accuracy-gated speed-accuracy operating point (M-SPEEDACC) that credits speed only when accuracy is held; and (c) engagement gating (M-ENGAGE) that certifies which trials - here and in other sections - reflect real effort. Absolute speed is reported as context, not as a tail decider.
age_rationale: A binary same/different tap needs only a point-and-press motor act, so it spans K-1 (large colored shapes differing by one feature, generous deadline) to 6-8 (3/6/9-digit strings and one-vs-many arrays, short deadline). Stimulus similarity and deadline - not motor demand - set the band, and young bands use oversized buttons to control the Fitts motor confound.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 two large shapes differing by color/shape -> 2-3 pictures differing by one added element -> 4-5 short 3-digit strings -> 6-8 long 6-9 digit strings and one-vs-many arrays
adaptive.difficulty_levers: stimulus similarity, string length, response deadline, mask on/off, proportion of 'same' trials
adaptive.notes: Items are procedurally generated (random strings / shape sets with a controlled number of mismatching features), giving effectively unlimited matched parallel forms for cross-item consistency (M-CONSIST).

engagement_hook: A fast 'twin or not?' arcade round with a smiley/frowny slam, a rising fast-and-correct combo, and a beat-your-streak meter.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Device latency/refresh inflates absolute RT (report device-robust RT variability over raw RT); touch vs mouse differences; visual acuity for fine string differences; a 'press same' response bias (mitigated by balancing trial types); large targets reduce motor (Fitts) noise.

name: Star Sweep
topics_techniques_covered: cancellation: tap every target (e.g., every apple) hidden among other pictures as fast and accurately as possible
cancellation: mobile cancellation that auto-scores hits, false alarms and a concentration-performance index
cancellation: scan rows and mark a conjunction target (a letter d carrying exactly two marks) while ignoring foils
cancellation: structured vs random arrays of picture/letter targets under a time limit
one_liner: A field fills with pictures and the child taps every target as fast as they can while never tapping a non-target.
interaction: A grid/field of target and distractor icons renders; the child taps targets to pop them (they mark as hit). Tapping a distractor logs a false alarm and shatters the combo shield. A block ends on a time budget or when all targets are cleared. Only tapping — no drag, no text.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a hand tapping two targets (which pop) and hovering over a distractor then pulling away (leaving it). One unscored warm-up field with immediate hit/false-alarm feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: Cancellation ability is best captured by combining detections with false-alarm control, not raw sweep speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score CPI = hits - false alarms and gate the combo on correct rejections (M-FALSEALARM, M-COMBO).
learning_science.source: Brickenkamp, R., & Zillmer, E. (1998). The d2 Test of Attention. Hogrefe & Huber.

learning_science.why: Performance drifts as time-on-task grows, so late lapses can bias a speed estimate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log accuracy/RT drift across the field (M-DRIFT) and discount disengaged late responses.
learning_science.source: Mackworth, N. H. (1948). The breakdown of vigilance during prolonged visual search. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1(1), 6-21.

learning_science.why: Tap time depends on target size and spacing, a motor confound unrelated to processing speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Hold icon size and spacing constant and use large touch targets so speed reflects search, not motor difficulty.
learning_science.source: Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 47(6), 381-391.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Accuracy-gated speed combo
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Rewards sustained joint speed+accuracy rather than impulsive peak speed; a coach-resistant index of controlled processing efficiency that separates children who hold both at pace from those who trade one for the other.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Increment a streak on each response meeting BOTH a correctness check and a per-child adaptive RT band; reset to 0 on any error, false alarm, or timeout; store max streak and the streak distribution.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=30 speeded trials so streak length is estimable.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Commission / false-alarm rate
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Isolates impulsive fast-but-wrong responding so raw speed is never rewarded; separates careful-fast (able) from impulsive-fast responders and underlies the concentration-performance index.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Count taps on non-target/foil stimuli plus anticipatory responses faster than a plausible floor (<150 ms), divided by response opportunities.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=40 target/non-target events with a meaningful foil rate (>=30% non-targets).

tail_precision_rationale: Sweep speed alone is a poor tail signal, so scoring leans on the concentration-performance index (hits minus false alarms), the accuracy-gated combo (M-COMBO), and false-alarm control (M-FALSEALARM): careful-fast children separate from impulsive-fast ones. Drift (M-DRIFT) flags disengagement so any tail decision rests on sustained, engaged performance rather than a lucky fast burst; absolute sweep speed is collateral.
age_rationale: Tapping targets in a field is motor-simple and works from K-1 (tap apples among two fruit types, large icons) to 6-8 (conjunction targets among confusable foils). Field density and foil similarity - not motor demand - set the band; young bands use fewer, larger icons and a picture (non-reading) target.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 tap apples among two fruit types -> 2-3 tap one picture target among 3-4 foils -> 4-5 letter/shape target among similar foils -> 6-8 conjunction target (d with exactly two marks) among confusable foils
adaptive.difficulty_levers: field density, target:distractor ratio, foil similarity, single-feature vs conjunction target, time budget
adaptive.notes: Fields are generated from a target/foil grammar with known hit/false-alarm keys, so CPI and combo score automatically and unlimited matched fields can be cloned.

engagement_hook: A satisfying 'pop every star' sweep with a combo that only grows on clean taps and a shield that shatters on a wrong tap.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Screen size limits field density; motor speed and tap accuracy (mitigated by large icons and constant spacing); prior game familiarity (mitigated by ghost-hand + warm-up); reading is avoided by using picture targets at young bands.

name: Secret Decoder
topics_techniques_covered: coding_digit_symbol: on-screen DSST where a 1-9 symbol key sits on screen and the child taps the symbol matching each presented digit
coding_digit_symbol: match each picture to its partner shape using a small two-row key, as many pairs as possible before time runs out
coding_digit_symbol: copy the symbol corresponding to each geometric shape or number using a printed key
coding_digit_symbol: scrolling digit-symbol substitution scoring correct matches and average time per correct match
one_liner: Using a visible key, the child taps the symbol that matches each incoming digit/shape, decoding as many as possible before the timer runs out.
interaction: A fixed key (digit/shape -> symbol pairs) sits at the top. A single prompt digit/shape appears in a slot; the child taps the matching symbol from a response row beneath. A correct tap advances to the next prompt; a wrong tap flashes red and stays until corrected. Tapping only; key stays visible.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the prompt digit, the hand tracing up to that digit in the key, then tapping the matching symbol below (which locks in). One unscored warm-up match with the key highlighted precedes the timed block.

learning_science.principle: Digit-Symbol / Coding as a processing-speed marker
learning_science.why: Symbol substitution under time is a long-validated index of clerical/processing speed in child batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: On-screen coding with a fixed visible key; score correct matches per unit time plus per-match consistency.
learning_science.source: Wechsler, D. (2014). WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual (Coding / Processing Speed Index). Pearson.

learning_science.why: Consistency of substitution speed tracks ability better than the single fastest match.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Emphasize RT variability and slow-tail lapses across matches (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE), not peak match speed.
learning_science.source: Coyle, T. R. (2003). A review of the worst performance rule. Intelligence, 31(6), 567-587.

learning_science.why: Looking between a distant key and the item adds load, so a novel child may fail for layout reasons rather than speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep the key and item on one screen and teach via a ghost-hand look-up plus one warm-up match.
learning_science.source: Chandler, P., & Sweller, J. (1992). The split-attention effect as a factor in the design of instruction. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 62(2), 233-246.

tail_precision_rationale: Coding throughput has low standalone tail discrimination and is coachable, so the sharper signals are substitution consistency (M-RTVAR) and slow-tail lapses (M-LAPSE) on correct matches, plus the speed-accuracy point (M-SPEEDACC). Randomizing the key each session blunts practice inflation. Its tail value is mainly as corroborating efficiency and engagement evidence, not a primary separator.
age_rationale: Coding requires holding a key and cross-referencing, so it starts at 2-3 (3-4 picture-symbol pairs, mirroring WISC Coding Form A used at ages 6-7) and extends to 6-8 (full 1-9 digit-symbol). It is excluded from K-1 because key cross-referencing - not motor speed - would dominate and unfairly penalize kindergarteners.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 three-to-four picture-symbol pairs -> 4-5 six digit-symbol pairs -> 6-8 full 1-9 digit-symbol key
adaptive.difficulty_levers: key size (number of pairs), symbol confusability, key always-visible vs briefly hidden (adds working memory), time budget
adaptive.notes: Key mappings are randomized per session (anti-practice); correct/incorrect is deterministic from the key, so parallel forms are unlimited.

engagement_hook: A spy 'crack the code' race against a shrinking timer with a live decode counter and a combo chain for clean fast matches.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Split-attention/layout load if key and item are far apart (kept adjacent); symbol confusability and fine motor for small targets (large targets used); practice/familiarity with coding (key randomized per session); no reading beyond digit/shape recognition is required.

name: Target Hunt
topics_techniques_covered: symbol_search: arcade tap-the-target with a visible accuracy meter; the combo builds only on correct AND fast taps and breaks on any false alarm
symbol_search: look at a target shape, then tap it when it appears among distractors sliding across, ignoring non-matches
symbol_search: scan a search group and mark whether either of two target symbols is present, row by row against the clock
symbol_search: visual search where RT and accuracy scale with set size and target-distractor similarity
one_liner: A target symbol is shown, then shapes stream across a lane and the child taps only the ones that match, as fast as possible without hitting foils.
interaction: One or two target symbols pin to the left. Symbols then slide across a lane; the child taps matches before they exit (a hit pops them) and must not tap foils (a false alarm). A visible accuracy meter and combo update live. Tapping only; a block runs on a timer.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the pinned target, a matching symbol sliding in and the hand tapping it (pop), then a foil sliding by while the hand deliberately does not tap. One unscored warm-up lane with feedback precedes scoring.

learning_science.why: RT rises with the number and similarity of distractors, giving a graded, calibratable difficulty lever.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scale set size and target-distractor similarity to titrate difficulty and log RT against set size.
learning_science.source: Treisman, A., & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97-136.

learning_science.why: An arcade tap task invites impulsive taps, so false alarms must cost more than a hit rewards.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The combo builds only on correct+fast taps and breaks on any false alarm (M-COMBO, M-FALSEALARM, M-SPEEDACC).
learning_science.source: Wickelgren, W. A. (1977). Speed-accuracy tradeoff and information processing dynamics. Acta Psychologica, 41(1), 67-85.

learning_science.why: The tap-only-matches rule must be obvious without any text.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost-hand taps a matching symbol and visibly ignores a foil before scoring starts.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., & Cooper, G. A. (1985). The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra. Cognition and Instruction, 2(1), 59-89.

tail_precision_rationale: Search speed is weakly diagnostic on its own, so the tail contribution is the joint speed-accuracy operating point under an accuracy gate (M-SPEEDACC, M-COMBO) and false-alarm suppression (M-FALSEALARM), which distinguish controlled fast search from impulsive tapping. The set-size RT pattern adds a rate signal, but absolute speed is treated as collateral rather than decisive.
age_rationale: Scanning for a held target among distractors needs stable comparison, appropriate from 2-3 (distinct shapes, small set size, slow slide) to 6-8 (two similar target symbols, larger sets, fast slide). K-1 is excluded because abstract-symbol search confounds speed with an emerging comparison skill; K-1 speed is captured instead by the matching, sweep, whack, and naming types.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 tap a distinct shape among 2 foils -> 4-5 more foils at moderate similarity -> 6-8 two target symbols among many confusable foils (WISC Symbol Search-like)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: set size, target-distractor similarity, slide speed, number of simultaneous targets, foil rate
adaptive.notes: Symbols are drawn from a large glyph pool with a tunable similarity metric, giving unlimited matched forms.

engagement_hook: An arcade lane where targets slide by and you snipe only the matches; the accuracy meter and combo reward clean, fast hits and punish trigger-happy taps.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Impulsivity inflating false alarms (penalized via combo break); slide speed interacts with device frame rate; target-distractor similarity must be perceptually calibrated; large targets limit the motor confound.

name: Whack-It
topics_techniques_covered: simple_reaction_time: arcade whack-it - tap the critter the moment it pops up; the combo rewards fast AND correct hits while tapping an empty hole breaks it
simple_reaction_time: press the instant a single stimulus appears over many trials; record mean and (critically) RT variability
choice_reaction_time: tap the left or right target depending on which side a friendly animal appears (two-choice)
choice_reaction_time: choice reaction across 1/2/4 alternatives; the slope of RT against log2(choices) indexes processing rate (Hick's law)
choice_reaction_time: derive intra-individual RT variability and lapse frequency per the worst-performance rule
one_liner: Critters pop out of holes and the child taps them the instant they appear (or taps the correct hole), with peeking-too-early penalized.
interaction: One or more holes are shown. After a jittered delay a critter pops from a hole; the child taps it (simple RT) or taps the hole it appeared in (choice RT). A tap before the pop is a false start; too slow is a miss. Feedback flashes, then the next trial. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a critter popping and the hand tapping it fast (combo ticks up), then the hand tapping too early and the combo breaking. One unscored warm-up pop precedes the scored block.

learning_science.why: Choice RT increases linearly with log2(number of alternatives), and that slope indexes information-processing rate.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer 1/2/4 holes as difficulty levers and derive the RT-vs-log2(N) slope (M-HICKSLOPE), separating central rate from a motor/device intercept.
learning_science.source: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 4(1), 11-26.

learning_science.why: Intra-individual RT variability and lapses predict ability better than mean or fastest RT.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Emphasize RT CV and slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE); never score peak speed.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A 'worst performance' analysis of individual differences. Intelligence, 14(3), 309-325.

learning_science.why: Very fast 'responses' before the stimulus are guesses, not perception.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Flag responses under 150 ms as false starts (anticipations) that break the combo and are excluded from RT (M-FALSEALARM).
learning_science.source: Luce, R. D. (1986). Response Times: Their Role in Inferring Elementary Mental Organization. Oxford University Press.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Hick's-law RT slope
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: A device- and base-motor-robust estimate of information-processing RATE: the intercept absorbs motor/device latency while the slope reflects central processing, so it is less confounded than absolute RT at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Administer blocks at 1, 2, and 4 response alternatives; regress mean correct RT on log2(N) and store slope and intercept.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=15 correct trials per set size (>=45 total) for a stable slope.

tail_precision_rationale: Peak reaction time is famously weak and confounded, so this type deliberately scores the parts of the RT distribution that DO track ability: intra-individual variability and slow-tail lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE; worst-performance rule) and the Hick slope (M-HICKSLOPE), whose intercept absorbs motor/device latency so the slope is a cleaner central-rate estimate. Anticipations are flagged (M-FALSEALARM). Even so its standalone tail power is modest and is framed as one converging signal.
age_rationale: Detecting and tapping a pop-up is the most motor-basic speeded act, so simple RT fits K-1 (one hole, huge target). Choice RT (two then four holes) is layered for 2-3 through 6-8 to derive the Hick slope. Target size is held constant across bands to control the motor (Fitts) confound.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 one hole (simple RT) -> 2-3 two holes (2-choice) -> 4-5 four holes -> 6-8 four holes with a short deadline and catch (no-pop) trials
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of holes (Hick N), inter-stimulus interval jitter, response deadline, proportion of catch trials
adaptive.notes: Trials are fully parametric (N, ISI, deadline); the RT-vs-log2(N) slope is computed across blocks and stimuli are trivially cloneable.

engagement_hook: Whack-the-critter the instant it pops - too eager (a false start) breaks your combo, so cool, precise timing wins the streak.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Anticipatory false starts (flagged <150 ms); device input latency (report variability and the Hick slope, whose intercept absorbs device/motor latency); touch vs mouse differences; fatigue on long blocks (drift logged).

name: Blink Towers
topics_techniques_covered: inspection_time: two lines/towers of different length flash briefly then are masked; report which side was longer (motor-free perceptual intake)
inspection_time: two towers flash then vanish behind a mask; the child taps the taller tower afterward at their leisure; accuracy at very short exposures is the index
inspection_time: backward-masked brief discrimination presented as a motor-free index of perceptual intake speed
one_liner: Two towers flash for a split second and are then hidden by a mask; the child calmly taps which one was taller, with the flash getting shorter each round.
interaction: Two towers appear for a staircased exposure, then a pattern mask overwrites them. Only after the mask does the child tap the taller side (a large LEFT / RIGHT choice). The response itself is untimed (motor-free); the manipulated variable is the pre-mask exposure. Tapping only.
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows the towers flash, the mask drop, and the hand calmly tapping the side that was taller (checkmark), emphasizing that answering is unhurried. One unscored warm-up with a long exposure precedes the staircase.

learning_science.why: The exposure needed to discriminate a masked stimulus correlates (modestly) with g and is largely motor-free.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Backward-masked two-tower discrimination with an untimed response; estimate the exposure threshold (M-ITTHRESH).
learning_science.source: Deary, I. J., & Stough, C. (1996). Intelligence and inspection time. American Psychologist, 51(6), 599-608.

learning_science.why: Sets honest expectations: inspection time is a real but modest correlate, best used as one signal among many.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Report the IT threshold as a motor-robust adjunct, never as a standalone tail decider.
learning_science.source: Grudnik, J. L., & Kranzler, J. H. (2001). Meta-analysis of the relationship between intelligence and inspection time. Intelligence, 29(6), 523-535.

learning_science.why: The mask removes the stimulus so motor/response speed cannot inflate the score.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present a pattern mask after a staircased exposure and let the child answer at leisure (motor-free).
learning_science.source: Vickers, D., Nettelbeck, T., & Willson, R. J. (1972). Perceptual indices of performance: A theory and its application to the study of intelligence. Perception, 1(3), 263-295.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Inspection-time threshold
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: A near motor-free, practice-resistant index of perceptual intake speed - the processing-speed measure with the cleanest (still modest) link to g and the least motor/device confound, making it the most defensible single speed adjunct at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Staircase the pre-mask exposure duration (e.g., 2-down/1-up) in a backward-masked two-alternative discrimination and estimate the exposure at the target accuracy (~71-75% correct).
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=40-60 masked trials for a stable staircase threshold; report threshold in ms alongside the measured display frame time.

tail_precision_rationale: Inspection time is the least motor- and practice-confounded speed measure and has the cleanest (still modest, r approx -0.3 to -0.5) link to g, so its threshold (M-ITTHRESH) is the most defensible single processing-speed tail adjunct - useful precisely because the response is untimed and motor-free. It is offered as a corroborating perceptual-intake index, never as a standalone tail decider.
age_rationale: The masked-discrimination response is untimed and motor-free, so difficulty is perceptual, not motor. It fits 2-3 (large height difference, long ~300-400 ms exposures) to 6-8 (small differences, short staircased exposures). At 2-3 exposures stay long and data are noisier, so it serves mainly as engagement plus a coarse perceptual screen; K-1 is excluded because understanding the flash-then-mask rule is unreliable that young.

adaptive.content_range: 2-3 large height difference, ~300-400 ms exposure -> 4-5 moderate difference, ~150-250 ms -> 6-8 small difference, staircased down toward ~30-80 ms
adaptive.difficulty_levers: pre-mask exposure duration (staircase), height-difference magnitude, mask strength, inter-trial interval
adaptive.notes: A 2-down/1-up staircase converges on the ~71% threshold; the two bars are generated, so items are infinitely cloneable and the threshold is a single robust statistic.

engagement_hook: A blink-and-you-miss-it towers duel: the flash gets shorter every round and you still have to call the taller tower - how short can you go?
construct_irrelevant_risks: Display refresh rate limits the shortest true exposure (report the threshold with the measured frame time); ambient brightness and visual acuity; sustained-attention lapses; but it is the least motor-confounded speed task because the response is untimed.

name: Speed Namer
topics_techniques_covered: rapid_automatized_naming: name a grid of repeated color patches (red, blue, green, black) as fast as possible - a pre-literacy naming-speed measure
rapid_automatized_naming: name a grid of repeated familiar objects (ball, dog, star) left-to-right as fast as possible; score is total time and errors
rapid_automatized_naming: rapid letter/digit naming as fast as possible; alphanumeric RAN most linked to reading fluency
rapid_automatized_naming: contrast serial (full-grid) naming, which requires sustained scanning and eye-movements, against discrete naming
one_liner: The child moves left-to-right across a grid of repeated items, tapping each as they name it aloud, keeping a smooth, fast rhythm.
interaction: A serial grid of repeated items renders. The child names each item aloud and taps it to advance (tap-to-advance), moving strictly left-to-right, top-to-bottom; the current item is highlighted. Each tap timestamps the inter-item interval. Total time, rhythm, and hesitations are logged. (Optional on-device speech can supplement, but tapping is the scored channel.)
self_teach: A <=10s wordless ghost-hand loop shows a hand tapping across the first row in a steady beat with a little 'speech' puff over each item, then continuing to the next row. One unscored warm-up row precedes the scored grid.

learning_science.why: Serial naming speed of familiar items is a robust correlate of reading fluency and processing speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a serial grid of repeated colors/objects/letters/digits and score total time plus inter-item rhythm.
learning_science.source: Norton, E. S., & Wolf, M. (2012). Rapid automatized naming (RAN) and reading fluency: Implications for understanding and treatment of reading disabilities. Annual Review of Psychology, 63, 427-452.

learning_science.why: Serial (full-grid) naming captures the scanning and eye-movement demands that discrete single-item naming misses.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a full-grid serial layout with tap-to-advance to capture the serial rhythm and hesitations.
learning_science.source: Denckla, M. B., & Rudel, R. G. (1976). Rapid automatized naming (R.A.N.): Dyslexia differentiated from other learning disabilities. Neuropsychologia, 14(4), 471-479.

learning_science.why: Inter-item pauses, not peak articulation speed, carry much of the naming-ability signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log inter-item-interval variability and long hesitations as lapses (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) rather than crediting the single fastest item.
learning_science.source: Kail, R., & Hall, L. K. (1994). Processing speed, naming speed, and reading. Developmental Psychology, 30(6), 949-954.

tail_precision_rationale: Naming speed predicts fluency more than g, so its tail value is narrow: rhythm consistency (M-RTVAR) and hesitation/lapse frequency (M-LAPSE) across the serial grid, plus drift (M-DRIFT), index automaticity and sustained engagement. It is best read as collateral fluency/effort evidence and a screen for disfluency, not as a gifted-tail separator.
age_rationale: Tap-to-advance serial naming needs only sequential taps, so it spans K-1 (5 colors or objects - pre-literacy naming) to 6-8 (letters/digits, denser grids). Content, not motor demand, sets the band: pre-readers name colors/objects while readers name letters/digits.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 grid of 5 repeated colors or objects -> 2-3 letters/digits in a 5x5 grid -> 4-5 denser mixed alphanumeric -> 6-8 dense letter/digit grids
adaptive.difficulty_levers: item type (color/object vs letter/digit), grid density, item confusability, row length
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated from an item pool; tap-to-advance yields rhythm and hesitation metrics without requiring voice capture, though optional on-device speech can corroborate.

engagement_hook: A rhythm run: name and tap across the grid to keep a smooth beat - hesitations break the groove and your rhythm meter shows it live.
construct_irrelevant_risks: True RAN requires voice capture; tap-to-advance is a serial-scanning proxy that could be gamed by tapping without naming (mitigated by rhythm-consistency checks and optional on-device speech); item familiarity/reading level (colors/objects for pre-readers); a motor tapping-speed floor.

name: Number Line Navigator
topics_techniques_covered: number-line estimation: locate a target number on a bounded line
place a point or fraction at the correct location on a number line
interpret the value of a point marked on a number line
one_liner: The child slides a marker to where a target number, fraction, or point belongs on a number line and releases to lock it in.
interaction: A horizontal number line is shown with labeled endpoints (sometimes one interior anchor). A target (numeral, fraction, pictured quantity, or a 'read this point' prompt) appears above. The child drags a glowing marker along the line and releases; the release position is the answer. For read-the-point variants the child instead taps one of 3-4 candidate values. Submission = release of the drag (auto-commit) with a ~1.5s undo/redrag window, plus a Lock button to confirm early.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<8s): a translucent hand grabs the marker, glides it to a lit target zone under the numeral 5 on a 0-10 line, and releases with a snap and chime; the target then changes and the hand repeats once. One unscored warm-up asks the child to place 2 on a 0-10 line with a wide green success band and gentle nudge arrows, so the drag-and-release mechanic is obvious with zero text.

learning_science.why: Number-line estimation accuracy (linear vs logarithmic placement) is one of the most robust behavioral predictors of broad math achievement and reveals the precision of a child's internal magnitude representation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score continuous placement error (percent absolute error), not just right/wrong, and shift endpoints and scale to probe the linearity of the child's representation.
learning_science.source: Siegler & Opfer (2003), 'The development of numerical estimation: Evidence for multiple representations of numerical quantity', Psychological Science 14(3):237-243.

learning_science.why: Beginning with a concrete, manipulable representation and fading toward symbolic form supports transfer and lets young children reason about magnitude before mastering symbols.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses a picture counting track; older bands fade to bare labeled lines with fractions, decimals, and negatives using the same drag mechanic throughout.
learning_science.source: Fyfe, McNeil, Son & Goldstone (2014), 'Concreteness fading in mathematics and science instruction', Educational Psychology Review 26:9-25.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Placement error (percent absolute error)
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Continuous placement error turns a single number-line item into a fine-grained latent-magnitude signal; small, consistent PAE at hard scales (fractions, wide ranges) separates top reasoners far better than dichotomous accuracy and avoids ceiling.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Record released position, convert to a value, compute absolute(placed - target) / line-range as a percent per item; also fit the child's placement curve (linear vs log R^2).
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=10-15 placements spanning the scale for a stable PAE and linearity estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: PAE plus placement-curve linearity give a continuous ability index that keeps resolving differences after accuracy saturates; first-action latency and revision count separate reflective, confident placers (plan then commit) from guess-and-adjust behavior at the same accuracy, adding process variance exactly where gifted candidates cluster.
age_rationale: Drag-and-release on a large line is within K-1 motor range given a wide success tolerance; tolerance tightens and content shifts (0-10 counting to 0-100/0-1000, then fractions/decimals/negatives, then proportional scales) rather than changing the interaction, so one shell spans all bands. Reading load is near-zero (numerals and points).

adaptive.content_range: counting and magnitude (0-10) through fraction, decimal, and negative placement and proportional scaling (6-8); the interactive line is the sponsor's example of one shell spanning a huge content range without notation.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: scale/range, tolerance-band width, target type (whole/fraction/decimal/negative), presence or absence of interior anchors, hidden intermediate ticks, read-the-point vs place-the-point, and non-integer endpoints (e.g., 0 to 3/4).
adaptive.notes: Endpoints and targets are sampled programmatically; PAE thresholding drives adaptive escalation of scale difficulty.

engagement_hook: A 'lock it in' snap with a rising chime and a shrinking bullseye that rewards precision, so it feels like calibrating a dial rather than answering a math question.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor precision on tight tolerances (mitigate with age-scaled band widths and a redrag window); touch vs mouse pointer resolution (normalize tolerance to device); tick-counting shortcuts (sometimes hide intermediate ticks); ensure color-independent success cues.

name: Magnitude Duel
topics_techniques_covered: quantitative_comparison: greater / less / equal / cannot be determined
approximate number system dot-comparison: choose the array with more dots
symbolic magnitude comparison: choose the larger of two numbers
compare or order numbers, fractions, or decimals
one_liner: Two quantities flash side by side and the child quickly taps the side that is greater, or taps 'equal' or 'can't tell'.
interaction: Two panels appear (dot arrays, numerals, fractions, or short expressions). The child taps the larger panel; a center EQUAL button and, for older bands, a CAN'T TELL button handle ties and indeterminate cases. Response = single tap (no drag). Non-symbolic arrays are briefly shown then masked to force approximate comparison; symbolic items stay visible. A streak/combo builds on fast-and-correct taps and breaks on a wrong tap.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<7s): two clusters of fish appear, the hand taps the clearly-more side, a green pulse and points pop; it repeats once with numerals. One unscored warm-up uses an easy 2-vs-8 dot comparison so the tap-the-bigger rule is obvious without words.

learning_science.why: Non-symbolic magnitude discrimination acuity (the Weber fraction) is measurable pre-symbolically and correlates with current and future formal math achievement, letting young or low-literacy children demonstrate quantitative ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include flashed-then-masked dot arrays with an adaptive ratio and estimate the ratio at which the child crosses a threshold accuracy (the Weber fraction).
learning_science.source: Halberda, Mazzocco & Feigenson (2008), 'Individual differences in non-verbal number acuity correlate with maths achievement', Nature 455:665-668.

learning_science.why: In speeded comparison, response consistency (low variability) and the slowest responses are more diagnostic of ability than peak speed; rewarding raw speed would be coachable and construct-irrelevant.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the full RT distribution and credit accuracy-held speed via a speed-accuracy model; surface RT variability and lapses rather than the fastest tap.
learning_science.source: Coyle (2003), 'A review of the worst performance rule', Intelligence 31(6):567-587.

new_measurements_proposed.name: ANS acuity (Weber fraction)
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Estimates the finest numerical ratio a child can reliably discriminate; a less-coachable, low-literacy tail signal that keeps separating children when symbolic items would floor or ceiling, especially in K-1.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Adaptively vary the ratio of the two non-symbolic arrays (staircase), fit a psychometric function to accuracy-by-ratio, and report the Weber fraction w and its standard error.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=30-40 non-symbolic trials spanning ratios ~1.1 to 2.5 for a stable w.

tail_precision_rationale: Pairing a stable speed-accuracy operating point with RT variability and lapse rate (worst-performance) yields a less-coachable fluency index; the adaptive Weber fraction extends discrimination below the floor of symbolic items, so even children who ceiling on symbolic comparison remain separable by non-symbolic acuity.
age_rationale: Single-tap choice is the lowest motor demand of any type, suitable from K-1. Content escalates from dot arrays (no symbols) to numerals, then fractions/decimals, then expressions with cannot-be-determined logic (6-8); the tap interaction never changes and reading load stays minimal.

adaptive.content_range: non-symbolic subitizing/ANS (K-1) through fraction/decimal ordering and indeterminate symbolic comparison with unknowns (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: array ratio (Weber), symbolic vs non-symbolic, numeral magnitude/format (whole/fraction/decimal/negative), inclusion of equal / cannot-be-determined, exposure duration and masking, and size-vs-number congruency.
adaptive.notes: Trivially cloneable via numeric templates and array generators; a staircase on ratio/difficulty gives per-child adaptation.

engagement_hook: A fast arcade 'duel' with a combo meter: quick correct calls build a streak and a bad call breaks it, so it feels like a reflex game while covertly titrating magnitude acuity.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Speed pressure can induce impulsive fast-wrong responding (credit only accuracy-held speed; never reward raw speed); visual density/size can confound number (control dot area and include size-number-incongruent trials); keep equal and can't-tell buttons equally reachable to avoid position bias.

name: Number Series Stepping Stones
topics_techniques_covered: number_series: infer the rule of a number sequence and supply the next term
determine the missing number in a sequence
continue an early pictorial pattern or quantity sequence
pattern_completion: extend a repeating or growing pattern and state the rule
one_liner: A path of stepping stones shows a number sequence with one stone blank; the child works out the rule and sets the missing or next number.
interaction: A row of stones displays a sequence (pictures/dots for K-1, numerals for older). One stone is blank (next-term at the end or an interior missing term). The child sets the value by (a) tapping one of 4 candidate stones, or (b) using +/- steppers or a small keypad to dial the exact number, then taps the blank stone to place it. Submission = place/confirm. An optional 'show one more example' scaffold reveals a parallel worked series and is logged.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): stones read 2, 4, 6, ?; the hand hops along the stones showing the +2 gap as a glowing arc between each, then drops an 8 onto the blank stone with a splash; it repeats once with 1, 2, 3, ?. Unscored warm-up: 5, 6, 7, ? with candidate stones, so continue-the-pattern self-teaches wordlessly.

learning_science.why: Number-series completion is a classic marker of fluid and quantitative reasoning: the solver must induce a generating rule and project it, tapping relational reasoning strongly tied to general ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Design difficulty and distractors around rule type (constant difference, multiplicative, alternating, second-difference) and log error type to reveal partial rule induction.
learning_science.source: Holzman, Pellegrino & Glaser (1983), 'Cognitive variables in series completion', Journal of Educational Psychology 75(4):603-618.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity limits reasoning by development
learning_science.why: Younger children handle adjacent/perceptual relations while older children manage higher-order relations; one series shell can span this by adjusting relational complexity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses pictorial +1 growth (perceptual), older bands use multi-operation and second-order-difference rules (relational), with the same placement interaction.
learning_science.source: Halford, Wilson & Phillips (1998), 'Processing capacity defined by relational complexity', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 21(6):803-831.

tail_precision_rationale: Adaptive escalation of relational complexity yields M-DIFFREACH (the hardest rule the child cracks), the sharpest single tail statistic; error-type tagging (off-by-one vs wrong-operation vs additive-when-multiplicative) distinguishes near-miss latent ability from genuine rule failure, refining placement right at the cut.
age_rationale: K-1 uses pictorial/quantity growth with candidate stones (recognition, low motor and reading); 2-3 and up add steppers/keypad for exact entry; 6-8 use multiplicative, alternating, and second-difference rules. The stepping-stone placement is constant; only rule complexity and entry mode scale.

adaptive.content_range: count-on pictorial series (K-1) through geometric, alternating, and second-difference numeric series (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: rule type (additive/multiplicative/alternating/polynomial), step size, position of the blank (next vs interior), candidate vs free entry, number magnitude, and two interleaved rules.
adaptive.notes: Series generated from parameterized rule families; near-miss distractors auto-derived (off-by-step, wrong-operation).

engagement_hook: Hopping a character across stones to 'complete the bridge': placing the right number extends the path with a bounce, turning rule-finding into building a route forward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Keypad/stepper entry adds motor and numeral-formation load (offer candidate-tap mode for young or motor-limited children); ensure distractors are not guessable by position; require no reading; cap digits so handwriting/working memory is not the bottleneck.

name: Build-a-Number Blocks
topics_techniques_covered: decompose a multi-digit number by place value and reason about its structure
number_properties_reasoning: even/odd, factors, or creating the largest result
number_sense_magnitude; numeration: identify, compare, and represent numbers
one_liner: The child composes a target quantity by dragging base-ten blocks (or ten-frame dots) into a workspace, regrouping units into tens as needed.
interaction: A target is shown (a numeral, a pictured/audio quantity, or a goal like 'make the largest number' or 'make an even number over 50'). The child drags unit, ten, hundred, and thousand blocks (K-1: dots into ten-frames) into bins while a live total updates. Ten units can be tapped to regroup into a ten and vice-versa. Submission = Done when the total matches or best meets the goal. A decompose variant asks the child to split a given number into place-value parts.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): target 13; the hand drags one ten-rod and three unit-cubes into the tray as the counter climbs 10, 11, 12, 13 and locks green; then it taps ten loose cubes to snap them into a rod (regrouping) once. Unscored warm-up: make 5 with unit cubes. No words needed.

learning_science.why: Flexible composition, decomposition, and regrouping of multi-digit numbers is foundational number sense predicting later arithmetic and rational-number learning; manipulatives externalize the base-ten structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require genuine regrouping (10 units to 1 ten) and log whether the child composes efficiently or by brute single-unit counting, capturing structural understanding beyond the final total.
learning_science.source: Fuson (1990), 'Conceptual structures for multidigit numbers', Cognition and Instruction 7(4):343-403.

learning_science.why: Acting on concrete objects supports magnitude and place-value reasoning before symbolic fluency, lowering the notation barrier for young or struggling children.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Blocks are draggable manipulatives with a live symbolic counter that links enactive action to the symbol; K-1 uses ten-frames while older bands fade to place-value bins with decimals.
learning_science.source: Bruner (1966), 'Toward a Theory of Instruction', Harvard University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Efficiency-vs-optimal and the move path expose strategy: building 137 as 1 hundred + 3 tens + 7 units (place-value chunking) versus 137 loose units reveals structural mastery invisible in a right/wrong total; regrouping moves and revisions distinguish fluent, planful builders from trial-and-error at the tail.
age_rationale: Dragging blocks into bins is K-1 feasible with large targets and snap-to-bin. Content scales from ten-frames/units (K-1) to tens and ones (2-3), hundreds/thousands with regrouping (4-5), and decimals plus 'largest-number' and even/odd/factor goals (6-8). The interaction (drag + regroup-tap + Done) is constant.

adaptive.content_range: count/compose to 10 via ten-frames (K-1) through multi-digit regrouping, decimals, and number-property optimization goals such as 'largest even number from these digits' (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: target magnitude, number of place values, forced regrouping, decompose vs compose, goal type (exact match vs constraint optimization: largest/even/factor), decimal places, and limited block inventory.
adaptive.notes: Targets and inventories generated numerically; optimal solution known for M-EFF; constraint goals cover number_properties_reasoning.

engagement_hook: A tactile stacking-blocks sandbox where ten cubes snap into a rod with a click; building the number feels like play and the live counter makes progress visible and satisfying.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fine-motor drag load (large blocks, snap-to-target, generous hit areas); brute-force counting instead of place-value reasoning (capture via M-EFF/M-PATH rather than penalizing outright); avoid reading via numeral/picture/audio targets; limit inventory clutter to reduce visual search load.

name: Balance Beam Equivalence
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: choose the weight(s) that keep a balance scale in equilibrium (Figure Weights)
number_sentence_building: enter values to balance both sides of an equation
mathematical-equivalence items (meaning of the equal sign, e.g. 3+4=_+5)
one_liner: The child adds or removes weights (or numbers) on a pan balance to make both sides equal, discovering the value that keeps the beam level.
interaction: A pan balance tilts based on the true total on each pan. Pre-loaded weights, shapes, or numbers sit on each side; the child drags weights onto a pan or dials a value into an empty slot until the beam levels. The beam animates tilt in real time (the heavier side drops). Submission = Lock when level, or place the required missing weight. A Figure-Weights variant gives equivalences and asks which weight will balance the target.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the left pan shows 3 and the right shows 1, so the beam tilts left; the hand drags a 2 onto the right pan and the beam swings level with a settle and green glow; it repeats once. Unscored warm-up: one apple vs an empty pan, drag one apple to balance. The tilt makes 'make it level = make it equal' obvious with no words.

learning_science.principle: Relational understanding of the equal sign
learning_science.why: Many children hold an operational ('the answer comes next') view of '='; a relational view (both sides the same amount) uniquely predicts later algebra success, and a balance makes equivalence perceptual.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-canonical equivalence (e.g., 3+4 = _+5) on the pans so only relational reasoners succeed, and log operational-error signatures such as placing the running total in the blank.
learning_science.source: McNeil & Alibali (2005), 'Why won't you change your mind? Knowledge of operational patterns hinders learning and performance on equations', Child Development 76(4):883-899.

learning_science.why: Children progress through identifiable rules (weight-only, then distance, then integrated) on balance tasks, so the balance is a validated probe of reasoning level that scales from concrete to proportional/torque reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer weight-only balancing for young bands and distance/torque (arm-length) balancing for older bands to probe higher rule levels within one shell.
learning_science.source: Siegler (1976), 'Three aspects of cognitive development', Cognitive Psychology 8(4):481-520.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Relational-vs-operational equivalence signature
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Flags whether a child treats '=' relationally (balances both sides) or operationally (dumps a running total), a research-backed early separator of algebra-ready reasoning that dichotomous accuracy hides; concentrates information exactly where pre-algebraic talent emerges.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On non-canonical equivalence items, classify the child's first substantive placement/entry against known operational-error targets vs the relational solution, and record whether they self-correct.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 non-canonical equivalence items to reliably classify the child's dominant strategy.

tail_precision_rationale: Real-time tilt turns solving into a guided search, so efficiency and exploration reveal whether the child computes the needed value directly (few, targeted moves) or hunts by trial. M-EQREL captures the relational/operational distinction that specifically forecasts algebra readiness, giving a qualitative tail separator beyond correctness.
age_rationale: Treating the beam as an equivalence relation (both sides must match a total) is the construct of interest and is beyond most K-1 children as a reasoning task, so K-1 is excluded to stay honest. 2-3 balance small whole-number totals; 4-5 add missing-addend and multi-weight cases; 6-8 add distance/torque and non-integer/ratio balancing. The drag/dial interaction suits grade 2 and up.

adaptive.content_range: concrete whole-number balancing (2-3) through missing-addend equivalence, multi-term sums, and distance/torque proportional balancing that encodes linear relationships without notation (6-8), a shell reaching pre-algebra/algebra reasoning.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of weights/terms, canonical vs non-canonical equivalence, missing-addend vs free-balance, weight-only vs distance/torque, integer vs fractional weights, and number of unknown slots.
adaptive.notes: Pan contents generated from equivalence templates; the torque variant introduces multiplicative reasoning; optimal move count known for M-EFF.

engagement_hook: A physically satisfying wobble-and-settle: the beam swings and teeters as weights land, so getting it perfectly level delivers immediate, game-like physical feedback.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag motor load (snap-to-pan, large weights); pure trial-and-error using the tilt cue (capture strategy via M-PATH/M-EFF and include commit-blind items for tail separation); avoid text via shapes/numerals; ensure tilt is readable without relying on color.

name: Function Machine
topics_techniques_covered: pattern_completion: 'number machine' input-output task, infer the transformation rule and give the output
generalize a growing figural-number pattern to the nth case and justify the relationship
one_liner: The child feeds numbers into a machine, watches inputs turn into outputs, infers the hidden rule, and predicts the output for a new input or assembles the rule.
interaction: A cartoon machine shows an input hopper and an output chute with a visible table of in-to-out examples (e.g., 2->5, 3->7, 4->9). The child may drag a limited number of test numbers into the hopper to see outputs (free probes), then answers the scored prompt: dial/tap the output for a new input, OR assemble the rule from operation tiles (e.g., [x2][+1]). Submission = confirm answer or rule. The free-probe count and choices are logged.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): the machine shows 1->3 and 2->4; the hand drops a 3 in the hopper and a 5 pops out the chute (the +2 shown as two glowing dots added); then the hand dials 5 for input 4 correctly. Unscored warm-up: a +1 machine (1->2, 2->3, input 5 -> ?). The visible cause-effect self-teaches the infer-the-rule idea.

learning_science.why: Input-output 'function machine' reasoning develops the covariation and generalization at the heart of algebra, and children can reason functionally well before formal notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer both 'predict the output' and 'build the rule from operation tiles' so children can express a general rule without algebraic symbols, escalating to two-step and nth-term generalization.
learning_science.source: Blanton & Kaput (2011), 'Functional thinking as a route into algebra in the elementary grades', in Early Algebraization (Springer), pp. 5-23.

learning_science.why: Letting the child probe inputs turns rule induction into active hypothesis testing; the efficiency and informativeness of chosen probes indexes scientific reasoning and separates systematic from random explorers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Give a small budget of free test-inputs and log which probes the child chooses and how many before committing (informative vs redundant probing).
learning_science.source: Klahr & Dunbar (1988), 'Dual space search during scientific reasoning', Cognitive Science 12(1):1-48.

tail_precision_rationale: Probe efficiency (how few and how informative the test-inputs before a correct rule) is a strong strategy separator: gifted reasoners induce two-step rules from minimal evidence. M-DIFFREACH over one-step, two-step, and nth-term rules pinpoints the ceiling, and hint-free solving at high difficulty is stronger tail evidence.
age_rationale: Holding an input-output relation in mind and generalizing suits grade 2 and up with single-step additive rules; 4-5 adds multiplicative and two-step rules; 6-8 adds nth-term generalization and rule-building from tiles. The machine metaphor and drag/dial answer are constant. K-1 is excluded because rule induction over symbols exceeds typical readiness.

adaptive.content_range: single-step additive machines (2-3) through two-step linear rules and nth-term generalization that is algebra reasoning without notation (6-8), one shell spanning pattern to pre-algebra.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: rule arity (one/two-step), operation set (+,-,x,divide), number size, predict-output vs build-rule, number of visible examples, free-probe budget, and near vs far transfer (next term vs 10th/nth term).
adaptive.notes: Rules sampled from parametric families; distractors from common mis-rules (one step applied only, swapped operations).

engagement_hook: A whirring contraption that visibly transforms numbers; dropping test numbers to 'crack the machine's secret' turns algebra into a detective and tinkering game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Working-memory load from tracking examples (keep the example table visible); no reading required (numerals + iconic operation tiles); guessing on predict-output (mitigate with build-the-rule items and probe logging); cap arithmetic size so computation is not the reasoning bottleneck.

name: Number Analogy & Matrix
topics_techniques_covered: number_analogies: infer the quantitative relation in a 2x2 and complete it
numeric_matrix: find the missing number that satisfies a matrix of relations
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: verbal and nonverbal number problems and patterns
relational reasoning across rows and columns
one_liner: The child finds the quantitative relationship linking numbers in a 2x2 pair (or 3x3 grid) and supplies the missing number that fits the same relation.
interaction: A 2x2 (A:B :: C:?) or a 3x3 grid of numbers is shown with one cell blank. The child determines the relation across and/or down and answers by tapping one of 4 candidate numbers or dialing the value on a keypad, then confirms. For the matrix both the row and column relations must hold. Submission = confirm. A 'peek' scaffold can reveal the row relation once and is logged.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<9s): 2:4 :: 3:? with a glowing 'x2' arrow drawn from 2 to 4; the same arrow then slides under 3 and the hand taps 6. Unscored warm-up: 1:2 :: 5:? with the mapping arrow shown. The animated relation-arrow teaches 'find what turns the top pair into each other, then apply it' without words.

learning_science.why: Analogies require mapping a relation from a source to a target rather than matching surface features; relational (vs attributional) responding marks higher reasoning and emerges with a relational shift in development.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Build distractors that are attractive on surface or additive grounds but wrong on the intended relation, so only true relational mappers succeed, and tag which relation each error implies.
learning_science.source: Gentner (1983), 'Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy', Cognitive Science 7(2):155-170.

learning_science.principle: Multiplicative relations develop later than additive
learning_science.why: Children default to additive relations before multiplicative ones; a number analogy readable either way separates children who access the multiplicative structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include items where an additive misread yields a specific logged wrong answer, isolating additive-vs-multiplicative reasoning at the tail.
learning_science.source: Vergnaud (1983), 'Multiplicative structures', in Lesh & Landau (eds.), Acquisition of Mathematics Concepts and Processes (Academic Press), pp. 127-174.

tail_precision_rationale: Error-type tagging separates additive misreads from random error and pinpoints latent multiplicative reasoners; cross-item consistency on matched (AIG-cloned) relations reduces the conditional standard error near the cut, so borderline children get more matched items before a decision, while M-DIFFREACH tracks the hardest relation family solved.
age_rationale: Explicit relational mapping over symbols suits grade 2 and up with simple additive relations and candidate answers; 4-5 introduces multiplicative relations and 3x3 matrices; 6-8 adds two-rule matrices and fraction/ratio relations. Tap/keypad answer is low motor. K-1 is excluded because symbolic relational mapping exceeds typical readiness.

adaptive.content_range: single additive 2x2 analogies (2-3) through multiplicative and two-rule 3x3 numeric matrices with fraction/ratio relations (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation type (additive/multiplicative/mixed), 2x2 vs 3x3, one vs two simultaneous relations, number magnitude/format, candidate vs free entry, and distractor design (additive foil present).
adaptive.notes: Relations sampled parametrically; matched clones support M-CONSIST; foils computed from common misreads.

engagement_hook: A glowing relation-arrow the child can replay to watch the transformation animate; solving feels like decoding a secret link between numbers rather than filling in a worksheet analogy.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Keypad entry adds motor and numeral load (offer candidate-tap for young bands); ensure distractors do not leak the answer by elimination; no reading required; keep magnitudes small so the bottleneck is the relation, not computation.

name: Ratio Mixer
topics_techniques_covered: proportional_reasoning: ratio/rate unit reasoning (e.g., exchange rate, best-buy comparison)
one_liner: The child adjusts quantities (scoops of two ingredients, or price vs amount) to match a target ratio or to pick the equivalent or better-value option.
interaction: Two connected quantities are shown as adjustable scoops/bars/sliders (e.g., a 2 red : 3 blue mixture, or a price for N items). The child either (a) adjusts one quantity so a second mixture matches the target ratio, with a 'taste-match' color meter showing closeness (not the numeric answer), or (b) taps which of two options is the better buy or equivalent ratio. Submission = Serve/confirm. Strategy (scaling both quantities vs adding a constant) is inferred from the move sequence.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a target glass is 1 red : 1 blue (purple); a second glass has 2 red, so the hand adds blue scoops one at a time until the color-match meter turns full green at 2 blue, then serves. Unscored warm-up: match 1:1 given one red already placed. The color meter teaches 'same ratio = same color' without numbers or words.

learning_science.principle: Proportional reasoning develops from additive to multiplicative
learning_science.why: Learners often misuse additive strategies on proportion problems; distinguishing multiplicative (ratio-preserving) from additive responders is a hallmark of higher quantitative reasoning and predicts later math.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use non-integer, non-doubling targets where an additive strategy gives a specific wrong mixture, and log whether adjustments preserve the ratio (multiplicative) or a difference (additive).
learning_science.source: Noelting (1980), 'The development of proportional reasoning and the ratio concept: Part I - Differentiation of stages', Educational Studies in Mathematics 11(2):217-253.

learning_science.why: Representing ratio as a perceptible quantity (color intensity, fullness) lets children reason proportionally before mastering fraction notation, broadening who can demonstrate the reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Render the ratio as a continuous perceptual cue (mixture color/needle) that reflects closeness to the target ratio without revealing the numeric answer.
