learning_science.source: Boyer, Levine & Huttenlocher (2008), 'Development of proportional reasoning: Where young children go wrong', Developmental Psychology 44(5):1478-1490.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Proportional strategy signature (multiplicative vs additive)
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Classifies whether the child preserves the ratio (multiplicative/scaling) or a constant difference (additive) during adjustments, the decisive divide in proportional reasoning that a correct/incorrect score cannot see; isolates genuine proportional reasoners at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: From the move sequence, fit whether successive adjustments hold the quantity-ratio constant vs the quantity-difference constant, classify the strategy, and record consistency across items.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 proportion items including non-integer/non-doubling targets to classify strategy reliably.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PROPSTRAT plus efficiency-vs-optimal separate multiplicative reasoners from additive approximators even when both eventually land correct, and non-integer targets prevent doubling shortcuts, concentrating discrimination on the reasoning that defines the upper tail of quantitative ability.
age_rationale: Robust proportional reasoning is later-developing; simple doubling can appear by grade 4, so 4-5 uses integer/doubling ratios while 6-8 uses non-integer ratios, rates, and best-buy comparisons. Slider/scoop adjustment is well within motor range. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because proportional reasoning is typically pre-emergent there, keeping coverage honest.

adaptive.content_range: integer/doubling mixtures (4-5) through non-integer ratios, unit-rate, and best-buy reasoning (6-8); the mixer shell reaches ratio/rate reasoning that normally needs fraction notation.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: integer vs non-integer target ratio, doubling vs non-doubling, number of parts, discrete scoops vs continuous slider, match-the-ratio vs pick-better-value, presence of an additive-trap distractor, and rate (per-unit) framing.
adaptive.notes: Targets generated as ratios; additive-trap answers computed; the perceptual meter is derived from ratio distance for M-PROG.

engagement_hook: A mixing/potion game where getting the ratio right turns the color exactly to the target and serves it; proportional reasoning becomes tuning a color rather than manipulating fractions.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The color meter could allow pure color-matching without numeric reasoning (include no-meter commit-blind scored items and log strategy); slider precision (snap to sensible increments, scale tolerance); avoid reading with iconic ingredients; provide non-color backups for color-vision differences.

name: Story Model Builder
topics_techniques_covered: model two growing quantities and find where they are equal (PISA Apples)
bar-model representation of a word problem
multi-constraint reasoning; short constructed numeric response
one_liner: The child builds a visual model (adjustable bars, two growing stacks, or tokens) of a short illustrated story problem and manipulates it to find the answer.
interaction: A short story is presented with icons and minimal or audio text (e.g., two plants growing at different rates). The child manipulates a model: drag to set bar lengths, step two quantities forward turn-by-turn, or place tokens to satisfy constraints, with a live readout of current values. For find-where-equal the child advances until the two quantities meet and marks that point; for bar-model problems the child sizes bars then reads or enters the answer. Submission = Answer with the modeled value; partial credit is captured from model correctness even if the final number is off.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): two seedlings; plant A starts at 2 and grows +1/day, plant B starts at 0 and grows +2/day; the hand taps 'next day' stepping both, the bars rise, and when they meet at day 2 (both = 4) a flag pops on the equal point. Unscored warm-up: step until a 1+1 stack equals a 2 stack. Watching the bars grow and meet teaches the find-where-equal goal wordlessly.

learning_science.why: Representing word-problem structure with proportional bars scaffolds reasoning about unknowns and relations without symbols and is a validated route to solving multi-step problems.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide draggable proportional bars as the response medium so the child expresses the problem structure, and score the model's structural correctness separately from the final number.
learning_science.source: Ng & Lee (2009), 'The model method: Singapore children's tool for representing and solving algebraic word problems', Journal for Research in Mathematics Education 40(3):282-313.

learning_science.why: Reasoning about how two quantities co-vary and when they coincide is core quantitative reasoning (the PISA Apples task) and predicts later functions and algebra understanding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include a 'two growing quantities, find where equal' interactive where the child steps time and observes the meeting point, capturing covariation reasoning directly.
learning_science.source: Carlson, Jacobs, Coe, Larsen & Hsu (2002), 'Applying covariational reasoning while modeling dynamic events: A framework and a study', Journal for Research in Mathematics Education 33(5):352-378.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial-credit scoring of the model (structure right, arithmetic slip) extracts tail information from one rich item like several dichotomous items and rescues near-miss latent ability; progress trajectory and persistence on hard multi-step items add a task-commitment signal (Renzulli) that pure accuracy misses, sharpening decisions among high performers who differ in how they push through difficulty.
age_rationale: Multi-step modeling and covariation reasoning require sustained working memory and inference typical from grade 4 up; 4-5 uses single-model, small-number problems while 6-8 uses multi-step, multi-constraint, and non-integer covariation. Audio narration removes decoding load. K-1 and 2-3 are excluded because multi-step model construction exceeds typical readiness, keeping coverage honest.

adaptive.content_range: single bar-model or small covariation problems (4-5) through multi-step, multi-constraint, and non-integer rate covariation (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of steps/constraints, integer vs non-integer rates, single vs multiple bars, magnitude, pre-structured vs built-from-scratch model, and audio vs text framing.
adaptive.notes: Story templates with swappable quantities/rates; partial-credit rubric tied to model structure; lower AIG cloneability than pure-numeric shells because narrative framing needs curation to avoid reading confounds.

engagement_hook: A story comes alive as a growing diagram the child controls; stepping time to watch two plants race and 'catch' the moment they are equal turns a word problem into an interactive animation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading/language load is the biggest risk (mitigate with icons, audio narration, and minimal text); working-memory load on multi-step items (keep live readouts visible); motor drag for bars (snap increments); the wordless demo must make the model buildable without prior bar-model schooling; the partial-credit rubric must not reward random dragging.

name: Turn-to-Match
one_liner: The child drags a shape around to spin it until it lines up with a rotated target outline, then locks it in.
interaction: Drag anywhere on the movable piece to rotate it about its center; it snaps to the nearest allowed angle (90 degrees for K-1, 45/30 degrees for older). When the piece overlaps the dashed ghost target within tolerance it snaps green and the LOCK button enables; tapping LOCK submits. A 3D multiple-choice shell instead asks the child to tap the one candidate that is a pure rotation (not a mirror image) of the target.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand grabs the piece, sweeps it around until it aligns with the dashed target, and it clicks green with a chime; then one unscored warm-up lets the child rotate-and-lock before any scoring.

learning_science.principle: Mental rotation is an analog, time-scaled internal transformation (chronometric)
learning_science.why: Response time rises roughly linearly with angular disparity, so rotation is a measurable process rather than a guess, and its rate indexes ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Vary target angular disparity across trials (45-180 degrees) and record RT against angle to estimate each child's rotation rate.
learning_science.source: Shepard & Metzler (1971), Science 171:701-703, 'Mental rotation of three-dimensional objects'.

learning_science.principle: Spatial-skill gaps shrink with familiar, manipulable formats and practice (malleability)
learning_science.why: Mental-rotation performance depends heavily on strategy and comfort, which self-teaching demos and direct manipulation equalize across groups.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a wordless ghost-hand plus free drag-to-rotate with snap so the score reflects rotation, not instructions or pointer precision.
learning_science.source: Uttal, Meadow, Tipton, Hand, Alden, Warren & Newcombe (2013), Psychological Bulletin 139(2):352-402, 'The malleability of spatial skills: a meta-analysis of training studies'.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Mental-rotation RT slope
new_measurements_proposed.what: Slope of correct-trial response time regressed on target angular disparity.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The classic Shepard-Metzler chronometric signature; a shallow slope held at high accuracy is a rate-of-mental-transformation measure that is hard to coach and finely separates the spatial tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Present matched trials at several angular disparities and regress correct-trial RT on angle per child.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=12 trials spanning >=3 disparities for a stable slope estimate.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Mirror false-alarm rate
new_measurements_proposed.what: Rate of selecting an enantiomorph (mirror-image) foil instead of a true rotation.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Distinguishes genuine 3D mental rotation from partial feature-matching; low mirror false alarms at high disparity is a clean tail separator.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Include exact mirror foils and log the chirality of the chosen distractor.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=8 trials that contain a mirror foil.

tail_precision_rationale: Angular-disparity RT slope (M-ROTSLOPE) and mirror false-alarm rate (M-MIRRORFA) separate children who truly rotate objects from those who feature-match; at the gifted cut a shallow RT-vs-angle slope held at high accuracy with near-zero mirror errors on 150-180 degree items (M-DIFFREACH) is a hard-to-coach signature that CogAT's spatial-light battery misses.
age_rationale: K-1 uses 2D single shapes, 90-degree snap, and large hit targets so limited fine-motor control never blocks a correct rotation judgment; 2-3 adds 45-degree snaps and mirror foils; 4-5 introduces 3D block figures at moderate disparity; 6-8 uses Shepard-Metzler 3D figures up to 180 degrees with mirror distractors. Precise free-hand angle setting is hard for young children, so snapping preserves the construct (rotation) while removing motor noise.

adaptive.content_range: 2D letter/shape rotation (K-1) to 3D multi-limb Shepard-Metzler figures at 180 degrees with mirror foils (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: angular disparity; 2D vs 3D; number of object limbs/segments; snap granularity; presence and similarity of mirror foil; time pressure
adaptive.notes: Figures and target angles are procedurally generated from a parametric shape plus a rotation matrix, and mirror foils are exact reflections, so unlimited matched clones exist at any fixed difficulty.

engagement_hook: Feels like turning a key or spinning a dial until it clicks; the satisfying green snap plus chime rewards precise alignment and invites 'just one more'.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor control (mitigated by snap and large targets); device (touch vs mouse rotation feel, normalize RT within device); familiarity with rotation games (mitigated by ghost-hand and warm-up); visual crowding for 3D figures (control limb count).

name: Shape-Fill Form Board
one_liner: The child drags loose puzzle pieces, rotating them when needed, to completely fill a target silhouette.
interaction: Drag each piece from the tray into the outline; a piece snaps into place when it is close and correctly oriented. A selected piece is rotated with a rotate handle or tap (snaps 45 degrees) and flipped for older bands. The item auto-submits when the silhouette is fully covered, or the child taps DONE; partial fills are scored by the fraction of area correctly placed.
self_teach: A ghost-hand drags one piece into the outline and it snaps with a click; a two-piece warm-up requiring no rotation precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Spatial assembly ('form board') is a distinct, strong marker of the visualization factor
learning_science.why: Composing parts into a whole taps figure-ground segmentation and mental transformation beyond simple perception.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use loose draggable pieces that fill a silhouette (a digital form board) rather than a 'which pieces fit' multiple-choice picture.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Manual for Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Form Board (VZ) marker tests.

learning_science.principle: Manipulatives externalize spatial reasoning and reduce working-memory load
learning_science.why: Physically moving pieces lets a child test partial solutions instead of holding them in mind, widening who can demonstrate the skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Allow free rearrangement and undo with snap-to slots so exploration is cheap and only strategy, not memory, is taxed.
learning_science.source: Newcombe (2010), American Educator 34(2):29-35, 'Picture this: increasing math and science learning by improving spatial thinking'.

tail_precision_rationale: Partial-area credit (M-POLY) plus placement efficiency (M-EFF: pieces placed vs re-dragged) and the placement sequence (M-PATH) turn one silhouette into a rich curve; strong solvers place large anchor pieces first and finish with few re-drags, so near-optimal assembly of a hard multi-piece silhouette at speed separates the tail even when several children all reach full coverage.
age_rationale: K-1 gets 2-3 large pieces, no rotation required, and a generous snap radius; 2-3 needs simple 90-degree rotations; 4-5 adds 45-degree rotations and more pieces; 6-8 uses 6-9 tangram pieces requiring rotation and reflection. Fine placement is removed by snapping so success reflects visualization rather than dexterity.

adaptive.content_range: 2-piece slide-together (K-1) to 9-piece rotate-and-reflect tangram silhouettes (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: piece count; rotation/reflection required; snap radius; silhouette ambiguity (multiple valid tilings); interior guide lines on/off
adaptive.notes: Silhouettes and piece sets are generated from a tiling engine, with difficulty set by number of pieces and required transformations; any complete tiling is accepted.

engagement_hook: Classic tangram/puzzle satisfaction: pieces click home and the silhouette lights up when complete, with a 'perfect fit' streak.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor drag precision (snap-to); rotation-control discoverability (ghost-hand shows the rotate handle); silhouettes with multiple valid solutions (accept any complete tiling, score coverage not one key).

name: Plan-the-Path
one_liner: The child guides a character from start to exit through a maze, and in harder items plans the shortest route that also collects required gems.
interaction: Drag the character, or tap adjacent cells / an arrow pad, to move it cell-by-cell along open corridors; walls block movement. Route-planning items require reaching the exit after collecting all gems, with a live move counter and a 'lock in route' commit for older children. The item completes when the character reaches the exit with all required gems collected.
self_teach: A ghost-hand traces the character smoothly from start through the turns to the exit; one warm-up on a tiny three-turn maze precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Route planning engages look-ahead planning (executive spatial function) beyond simple tracing
learning_science.why: Planning a multi-target shortest path taxes mental simulation of future states, a higher-order spatial component.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Add a plan-before-move, multi-gem, fewest-steps variant and score moves against the optimal path, not just completion.
learning_science.source: Shallice (1982), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298:199-209, 'Specific impairments of planning' (Tower of London paradigm).

learning_science.principle: Mazes are a long-validated child spatial/planning measure requiring foresight and impulse control
learning_science.why: Successful solving requires inhibiting the first move and planning ahead, a documented developmental spatial-executive marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Record first-move latency and dead-end entries as planning-vs-impulsive-tracing indices.
learning_science.source: Porteus (1965), 'Porteus Maze Test: Fifty Years' Application', Pacific Books.

tail_precision_rationale: First-move latency (M-RTFIRST) captures planning before acting, while path efficiency vs optimal (M-EFF) and dead-end re-entries (M-REV) reveal look-ahead depth; at the tail a long reflective pause followed by a near-optimal, backtrack-free route through a dense multi-gem maze (high M-DIFFREACH) is the plan-ahead signature that distinguishes gifted problem-solvers from fast trial-and-error tracers.
age_rationale: K-1 gets a large single-solution maze with few turns and finger-drag movement; 2-3 adds blind alleys; 4-5 introduces shortest-path with 1-2 gems; 6-8 uses dense mazes with multiple required targets and a fewest-steps budget. Wide corridors and snap-to-cell movement keep motor demand low across all bands.

adaptive.content_range: single clear path with few turns (K-1) to dense multi-gem shortest-path planning under a move budget (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; corridor branching / dead-ends; number of required gems; move budget vs optimal; plan-first (no free retrace) mode
adaptive.notes: Mazes are generated procedurally (DFS/Prim) with guaranteed solvability and a computed optimal-path length, so difficulty and the optimum for M-EFF scoring are known for every clone.

engagement_hook: A friendly character to steer, gems to grab, and 'stars for fewest steps' turn planning into a mini adventure.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (both drag and tap allowed, wide corridors); reading (none, fully wordless); rewarding speed over planning (credit efficiency and optimality, not raw time).

name: Build-the-Blocks
one_liner: The child reproduces a shown pattern by placing and rotating colored blocks into a grid (2D block design), scaling up to building a 3D model from a blueprint.
interaction: Drag tiles from a palette into grid cells; each tile can be rotated (tap or handle, snaps 90 degrees) and tiles include solid colors and diagonal two-color splits (classic block design). The grid cell snaps the tile in. For 6-8 the child instead builds a stack of unit cubes on an isometric board to match given front/side/top views. Scoring matches each cell or voxel to the target; DONE submits.
self_teach: A ghost-hand drags a tile in, rotates it once to match the card, and it snaps; a two-cell warm-up with solid colors only precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Block Design is a premier measure of visuospatial analysis (part-whole decomposition)
learning_science.why: Reconstructing a design requires segmenting the whole into block-sized units and mapping each block's orientation, a core spatial-analytic skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use rotatable diagonal-split tiles and score per-cell match so the task captures decomposition and orientation, not color memory.
learning_science.source: Wechsler (2014), WISC-V Technical and Interpretive Manual, Block Design subtest; Kohs (1920), Journal of Educational Psychology, 'The Block-Design Tests'.

learning_science.principle: Constructing to a target ('copy the model') externalizes spatial visualization linked to STEM
learning_science.why: Building tasks tap and predict the spatial skills that forecast later STEM achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Include an isometric build-to-blueprint variant for older bands to extend the range into 3D construction.
learning_science.source: Wai, Lubinski & Benbow (2009), Journal of Educational Psychology 101(4):817-835, 'Spatial ability for STEM domains: aligning over 50 years of cumulative psychological knowledge'.

tail_precision_rationale: Per-cell partial credit (M-POLY) with build trajectory (M-PROG) and rotation/placement efficiency (M-EFF, M-PATH) expose strategy: tail solvers decompose the design and place each block in near-minimal moves without churn (low M-REV). Reproducing a hard diagonal-split design or a 3D blueprint at speed with an efficient move path (high M-DIFFREACH) grades the top of the distribution beyond a right/wrong final score.
age_rationale: K-1 uses a 2x2 grid of solid-color tiles, no rotation, and big snap cells; 2-3 adds 90-degree rotation of diagonal tiles on a 2x2; 4-5 uses 3x3 designs; 6-8 uses 3x3+ designs and a 3D build-to-orthographic-views task. Snapping into cells removes placement dexterity so scores reflect analysis rather than aim.

adaptive.content_range: 2x2 solid-color copy (K-1) to 3x3 diagonal-split designs and 3D voxel build-to-blueprint (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: grid size; presence of diagonal-split tiles; rotations required; number of colors; 2D vs 3D (orthographic-view) target; time pressure
adaptive.notes: Target designs are generated by sampling a tile and rotation per cell; 3D targets are generated as voxel sets rendered to three orthographic views, giving unlimited matched clones.

engagement_hook: Tactile 'click the block in' building with a live match-meter that fills as the design comes together; Lego-like flow.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (snap cells); color vision (use distinct hue plus value or add patterns); rotation discoverability (ghost-hand demonstrates); device screen size for 3x3 grids.

name: Fold-the-Net
one_liner: The child folds a flat net up into a 3D box and works out which face ends up opposite a marked face.
interaction: The child scrubs a 'fold' slider (or taps FOLD) to animate the flat net closing into a 3D cube, then drags to rotate the finished cube in 3D to inspect all faces. To answer, the child taps the color/symbol swatch that is OPPOSITE the marked star face and taps LOCK. A multiple-choice net-to-solid matching variant (pick which cube the net makes) is offered as an alternate shell.
self_teach: A ghost-hand pushes the fold slider so the net closes into a cube and spins it once; a warm-up on a simple cube with an obvious opposite face precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Surface development (net folding) is a classic spatial-visualization factor test
learning_science.why: Mentally folding a 2D net into a 3D solid is a canonical marker of the visualization factor (VZ).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an actual fold animation the child controls plus free 3D rotation, then ask for the opposite or adjacent face.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Surface Development (VZ-3).

learning_science.principle: Interactive 3D exploration supports mental-model construction better than static pictures
learning_science.why: Folding and rotating lets a child build and check an internal 3D model, especially those with weaker static imagery.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Let the child scrub the fold and orbit the cube so exploration behavior itself becomes an observable strategy signal.
learning_science.source: Hegarty (2004), Learning and Instruction 14(3):343-351, 'Dynamic visualizations and learning: getting to the difficult questions'.

tail_precision_rationale: Exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE: how much the child scrubs the fold and orbits the cube) plus error type (M-ERRTYPE: adjacent-face near-miss vs random) reveal whether a correct answer came from a solid mental model or from manipulation-by-trial; tail solvers answer hard nets (more faces, asymmetric symbols) correctly with minimal orbiting (high M-DIFFREACH, low M-EXPLORE), indicating internal visualization rather than externalized search.
age_rationale: Mentally mapping a 2D net to a 3D solid exceeds most K-1 children (pre-operational limits on cross-dimensional transformation), so the type starts at 2-3 with a simple six-square cube and an obvious opposite face; 4-5 adds symbols on faces; 6-8 uses irregular nets, prisms/pyramids, and adjacency (not just opposite) questions. The controllable fold animation scaffolds younger children without giving away the answer.

adaptive.content_range: simple cube net, name the opposite face (2-3) to irregular prism nets with adjacency questions and multiple candidate solids (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: net regularity; solid type (cube to prism/pyramid); symbol vs color faces; opposite vs adjacent question; number of multiple-choice candidate solids; fold-scaffold on/off
adaptive.notes: Nets are generated from valid unfoldings of a chosen solid with a fixed face-adjacency map, so the correct opposite/adjacent face is computed automatically for any clone.

engagement_hook: Watching a flat cross fold itself into a box you can spin in your hands is inherently delightful; 'origami you control'.
construct_irrelevant_risks: 3D rotation control on touch (large orbit area, momentum off); animation giving away the answer (fold stops before revealing hidden faces unless the child chooses to orbit); symbol legibility.

name: Fold & Punch
one_liner: The child folds a paper one or more times, punches a hole, then predicts where all the holes will be once it is unfolded.
interaction: The child taps fold controls (fold left/right, top/bottom, or a diagonal for older) to animate the sheet folding, then taps a spot to punch a hole through all layers (shown on the folded stack). The child predicts the result by tapping cells on the unfolded grid where holes will appear, then taps CHECK/LOCK. In warm-up the sheet actually unfolds to reveal the truth; in scored items the child commits predictions first.
self_teach: A ghost-hand folds the sheet once, punches, then unfolds to show the two symmetric holes; one warm-up (single fold, one punch) precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Paper folding with punched holes is a benchmark spatial-visualization test
learning_science.why: Predicting the unfolded hole pattern requires mentally reversing folds and applying reflection symmetry, a core visualization operation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Have the child perform the folds and punches, then mark predicted holes on the unfolded grid as a constructed response rather than a four-option pick.
learning_science.source: Ekstrom, French, Harman & Dermen (1976), 'Kit of Factor-Referenced Cognitive Tests' (Educational Testing Service), Paper Folding (VZ-2).

learning_science.principle: A single wordless worked demonstration teaches a novel spatial rule faster than instructions (worked-example effect)
learning_science.why: Worked examples reduce cognitive load for novices, so the unfold-reveal teaches the reflection rule without text.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The warm-up performs one full fold-punch-unfold as a wordless worked example, then scored items withhold the reveal until after commit.
learning_science.source: Sweller, van Merrienboer & Paas (1998), Educational Psychology Review 10(3):251-296, 'Cognitive architecture and instructional design' (worked-example effect).

tail_precision_rationale: Scoring predicted-vs-true holes as graded overlap (M-POLY) and classifying misses (M-ERRTYPE: correct hole count but wrong reflection axis is a systematic near-miss vs random) extracts fine tail information from one item; the sharpest separator is accuracy on multi-fold, asymmetric-punch items (high M-DIFFREACH) where each extra fold doubles the required reflections, so able children track all layers while others lose a fold.
age_rationale: Reversing folds by reflection is beyond most K-1 children, so the type begins at 2-3 with a single fold and one punch on a coarse grid; 4-5 uses two orthogonal folds; 6-8 uses three folds including an oblique fold and multiple punches. Tapping large grid cells keeps motor demand minimal, and the live unfold in warm-up scaffolds the rule.

adaptive.content_range: single fold plus one punch on a 4x4 grid (2-3) to three folds including an oblique fold with multiple punches on a fine grid (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of folds; fold orientation (orthogonal vs oblique); number and position of punches; grid resolution; symmetric vs asymmetric layout
adaptive.notes: A fold sequence plus punch coordinates define the item; the true unfolded hole set is computed by reflecting punches across each fold axis in reverse order, so every clone is auto-keyed and partial credit is exact.

engagement_hook: Hands-on 'fold the paper, punch it, guess the surprise' with a satisfying unfold reveal; like a magic trick the child performs.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor (large grid taps); giving away the rule (reveal only in warm-up or after commit); grid-resolution ambiguity (snap punches to cell centers).

name: What Do They See
one_liner: The child figures out what a character sees from where it stands, by moving the character or pointing a dial toward a target from the character's viewpoint.
interaction: A small scene of labeled objects is shown from above with a character token. As the child drags the character around the scene (snapping to set viewpoints), a live 'what they see' strip updates, showing the objects in the character's left-to-right order. To answer, the child either drags the character to the spot that would produce a shown view, or (older bands) rotates a pointer dial to indicate the direction to a hidden target as seen from the character's heading, then taps LOCK.
self_teach: A ghost-hand walks the character to the other side and the 'what they see' strip flips left-to-right; a warm-up asks the child to match one simple two-object view before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Perspective taking (spatial orientation) is a spatial factor dissociable from object rotation
learning_science.why: Imagining a scene from another viewpoint (self-to-object) is separable from mentally rotating objects and predicts navigation ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score directional/heading error to a target from an imagined viewpoint, not object rotation, to isolate the perspective factor.
learning_science.source: Kozhevnikov & Hegarty (2001), Memory & Cognition 29(5):745-756, 'A dissociation between object manipulation spatial ability and spatial orientation ability'.

learning_science.principle: Young children default to their own view (egocentrism) and improve with concrete, movable viewpoints
learning_science.why: The three-mountains work shows perspective taking develops later, and letting children move a character scaffolds the viewpoint shift.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a live, movable character and start with 2-4 discrete viewpoints for younger bands rather than abstract heading estimation.
learning_science.source: Piaget & Inhelder (1956), 'The Child's Conception of Space' (three-mountains task), Routledge & Kegan Paul.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Perspective-taking angular error
new_measurements_proposed.what: Signed angular error between the child's indicated heading/direction and the true direction to the target from an imagined viewpoint.
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Grades perspective responses far more finely than right/wrong, and its systematic component quantifies residual egocentric bias; low angular error at large viewpoint offsets is a navigation-linked tail signal standard batteries omit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: On pointing/heading items, record the dial angle and subtract the geometric correct heading; decompose into random and egocentric-bias components.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=10 pointing trials across a range of viewpoint offsets for a stable error and bias estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: Continuous heading/pointing error (M-VIEWANG) grades responses far more finely than right/wrong, and its systematic component (pointing as if from the child's own position) quantifies residual egocentric bias; at the tail, low angular error on large viewpoint offsets (>=135 degrees) with little exploration (M-EXPLORE) marks children with a true allocentric model, a navigation-linked spatial strength standard batteries omit.
age_rationale: Robust allocentric perspective taking emerges around ages 6-8, so the type starts at 2-3 with only 2-4 discrete viewpoints and a live-updating view strip (recognition, not generation); 4-5 uses more objects and 4-8 viewpoints; 6-8 uses continuous pointing-dial heading estimation. The movable character gives concrete support so younger children are not blocked by pure imagery, and K-1 is excluded because egocentric responding dominates.

adaptive.content_range: match a two-object view among 2-4 viewpoints (2-3) to continuous dial heading toward a target from an imagined orientation (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of objects; number and spacing of viewpoints; discrete match vs continuous pointing; viewpoint offset magnitude; self vs array reference frame
adaptive.notes: Scenes are generated by placing N labeled objects at coordinates and the correct view/heading is computed geometrically, so items and keys clone automatically; works_well is 'med' because the construct's onset is late and floor effects appear before about age 6.

engagement_hook: A character with a live 'camera view' you control: move it around and watch the world reorder from its eyes; it feels like directing a scene.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor for young bands (report reliability, exclude K-1); reading (labels replaced by icons); motor (snap viewpoints, coarse dial detents for younger); mistaking left/right mirroring for error (score angular direction consistently).

name: Slice-It
one_liner: The child slides a cutting plane through a 3D solid and picks the 2D shape revealed at the cut.
interaction: A rotatable 3D solid is shown; the child drags a cutting-plane slider to move the slice up and down (and, for older bands, drags a tilt handle to angle the plane). A live outline previews where the plane meets the solid; the child then taps the matching 2D cross-section shape from an option row and taps LOCK. A concrete variant 'cuts' a familiar object (carrot, apple) and asks for the cut face.
self_teach: A ghost-hand slides the plane through a cylinder and taps the circle; a warm-up with a straight cut of a familiar object precedes scoring.

learning_science.principle: Cross-sectioning (penetrative thinking) is a spatial skill central to STEM
learning_science.why: Inferring the internal 2D shape of a 3D solid predicts and supports learning in geology, anatomy, and engineering, and is trainable.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use an interactive slice-and-reveal with adjustable plane height and angle rather than a single static picture.
learning_science.source: Cohen & Hegarty (2012), Learning and Individual Differences 22(6):868-874, 'Inferring cross sections: when internal visualizations are more important than properties of external visualizations'.

learning_science.principle: Dynamic, interactive visualization aids those with lower spatial imagery
learning_science.why: Moving the cutting plane supports building the internal model instead of requiring it in advance.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide a movable plane and rotatable solid and log how much the child explores before committing.
learning_science.source: Hegarty (2004), Learning and Instruction 14(3):343-351, 'Dynamic visualizations and learning: getting to the difficult questions'.

tail_precision_rationale: Exploration before commit (M-EXPLORE: plane moves and rotations sampled) and near-miss error typing (M-ERRTYPE: circle-for-ellipse on an oblique cut, or triangle-for-trapezoid) distinguish children who read the geometry from those who guess the 'obvious' shape; the tail signal is correct oblique cross-sections of prisms and cones (high M-DIFFREACH) answered with minimal plane-scrubbing, indicating internal penetrative visualization.
age_rationale: Predicting internal cross-sections is difficult before about age 9 and keeps improving through adolescence, so the type is scoped to 4-5 (concrete objects, straight axis-aligned cuts, few options) and 6-8 (abstract solids including prisms, cones, and pyramids with oblique cuts). It is excluded from K-1 and 2-3 because penetrative thinking is largely undeveloped and would floor.

adaptive.content_range: straight cut of a familiar object or cylinder, pick among 2-3 shapes (4-5) to oblique cuts of prisms, cones, and pyramids among close distractors (6-8)
adaptive.difficulty_levers: solid type; plane orientation (axis-aligned vs oblique); option-set similarity; concrete vs abstract solid; tilt control enabled
adaptive.notes: The correct cross-section is computed analytically per solid-and-plane pair for a library of solids; oblique and irregular solids require more authoring, hence medium cloneability.

engagement_hook: Slice through objects like a knife through fruit and watch the cut face appear; a 'reveal the hidden shape' mechanic that begs experimentation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Developmental floor (scope to 4-5 and up); 3D rendering legibility (clear edges, controllable rotation); plane-control discoverability (ghost-hand); distractor similarity tuned so guessing is penalized.

name: Word Safari
one_liner: Hear a spoken word and tap the one of four pictures that shows what it means.
interaction: Four picture tiles appear; a speaker button plays the target word (audio in production; play-button + text caption in this demo). The child taps one tile; the tile locks with a confirming pop. No printed words are read. Word rarity auto-adjusts up/down by a frequency staircase after each answer.
self_teach: Wordless ghost-hand demo (<10s): the speaker icon pulses, then a floating hand glides to the correct picture and taps it with a happy pop. Then one unscored warm-up uses an easy high-frequency word; any tap is accepted with gentle feedback before scoring begins.

learning_science.why: Pairing a spoken word with candidate pictures lets meaning be verified across verbal and visual codes, removing the reading load that would otherwise confound a young child's vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Prompts are audio; every response is a picture, never a printed word.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

learning_science.why: Vocabulary breadth spans a huge range, so presenting words near the child's current level yields the most information per item and reaches the individual ceiling efficiently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A frequency staircase raises/lowers word rarity (Zipf band) after correct/incorrect answers to locate the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH).
learning_science.source: Weiss, D. J. (1982). Improving measurement quality and efficiency with adaptive testing. Applied Psychological Measurement, 6(4), 473-492.

learning_science.why: For gifted screening, differences in print exposure or language background can masquerade as ability; leveling and lure design isolate the target construct.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors are matched on frequency and tagged as phonological / thematic / category lures so error meaning (M-LURETYPE) is separated from motor or guess noise.
learning_science.source: Haladyna, T. M., & Downing, S. M. (2004). Construct-irrelevant variance in high-stakes testing. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice, 23(1), 17-27.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Lexical frequency ceiling
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Vocabulary breadth is one of the strongest, most stable verbal-ability correlates; the rarest word-frequency (Zipf) band a child reliably handles separates gifted lexical depth once common words ceiling. An adaptive staircase individualizes the frontier, making it less coachable than a fixed word list.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Run an adaptive frequency staircase over frequency-tagged word items (receptive vocab, opposites/synonyms, context cloze); record the lowest-frequency (rarest) band answered correctly at criterion.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=15-20 adaptive vocabulary items spanning several frequency bands to localize the ceiling with acceptable error.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Distractor lure profile
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Which class of distractor (phonological cousin, category/semantic cousin, thematic associate, surface match) pulls a child's errors reveals the grain of their semantic/relational discrimination; category-cousin near-misses at high difficulty indicate latent ability just below the cut, refining placement beyond right/wrong.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag every distractor with a lure class; on each error log the lure class chosen; aggregate the per-child error-by-lure distribution.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Every incorrect response; requires items built with a designed lure taxonomy; >=10-15 errors for a stable profile (pooled across verbal types).

tail_precision_rationale: Vocabulary ceiling is one of the cleanest verbal tail separators: once high-frequency words are trivial for a gifted child, only the rarest words discriminate. The frequency staircase drives each child to their personal lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL / M-DIFFREACH) instead of stopping at grade level, while lure-type analysis (M-LURETYPE) confirms that near-misses at ceiling are fine semantic discriminations (category cousin) rather than random taps, adding resolution exactly at the cut.
age_rationale: Point-to-picture receptive vocabulary needs no reading and only a single tap, so it works from K-1. It is retained through 4-5 with rarer words, but above 4-5 a pure picture-vocab task tends to ceiling and loses tail information for gifted readers, where meaning-in-context (Story Quest, Fill the Gap) carries more signal; hence 6-8 is excluded by design.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete high-frequency nouns/verbs (K-1) through low-frequency and abstract words depicted via small scenes (4-5); frequency-leveled by Zipf band.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency/rarity; abstractness (concrete object vs depicted action/attribute); semantic closeness of distractors; number of tiles (2->4->6); audio-only vs audio+scene.
adaptive.notes: Items auto-generated from a frequency-tagged word bank paired with an image library; parallel forms cloned by swapping same-frequency words and same-lure-class distractors.

engagement_hook: A safari photo hunt: each correct tap snaps a photo of the animal/thing into a sticker album, and rarer words earn shinier stickers, so climbing the vocabulary ladder is the reward.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Highest verbal risk is language background and print exposure (mitigated by audio prompts, frequency leveling, and dialect-neutral imagery); image ambiguity (mitigated by prototypical pictures per Rosch); motor mis-tap (large tiles, lock-to-confirm, revisions logged via M-REV); device audio quality (caption fallback + replay button).

name: Bridge Pairs
one_liner: See a top pair of pictures that go together, then pick the picture that makes the bottom pair go together the same way.
interaction: A 2x2 matrix: top-left -> top-right shows a relation (bird -> nest); bottom-left is given and bottom-right is blank with four picture choices below. The child taps a choice; an arrow animates the mapped relation and the tile locks. Young bands hear the relation frame; older bands use printed frequency-leveled word pairs.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the top pair connects with a glowing arrow, an identical arrow starts from the bottom-left, and the hand taps the picture that completes the same arrow. One unscored warm-up (dog->puppy, cat->?) with an obvious relation runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Analogy is aligning relational structure rather than surface features; young children reason relationally when the relation is familiar and depictable, letting us measure fluid verbal reasoning with almost no vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Relations use concrete, cross-culturally familiar pairs (animal->home, object->function) shown as pictures, so the near-language-free relation carries the item.
learning_science.source: Gentner, D. (1983). Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy. Cognitive Science, 7(2), 155-170.

learning_science.why: Children as young as 3-4 solve a:b::c:d analogies when the relations are within their knowledge, so picture analogies validly bridge pre-readers to older verbal analogies.
learning_science.concrete_decision: K-1 uses picture relations; the identical shell swaps in printed frequency-leveled word pairs for 6-8, letting one type span all bands.
learning_science.source: Goswami, U. (1992). Analogical Reasoning in Children. Lawrence Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Zero written instructions and a single mapped arrow keep working memory on the relation instead of on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The animated arrow externalizes the relation frame; there is no instructional text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Because the relation, not vocabulary, carries the item, correct answers on multi-relation or abstract-relation analogies isolate fluid-verbal reasoning near the cut with minimal language confound. The distractor taxonomy (M-ERRTYPE: surface-match lure vs relational-reversal lure) reveals whether a near-miss reflects partial relational alignment (latent ability just under threshold) versus surface capture, and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) separates reflective mappers from guessers at ceiling.
age_rationale: Picture analogies with familiar relations are solvable from K-1 (single tap, no reading). The same shell scales to 6-8 by increasing relational complexity and switching pictures to printed frequency-leveled word pairs; motor demand stays a single tap throughout.

adaptive.content_range: One concrete relation (animal->baby) up to abstract/double relations (tool->action->product) and printed word analogies across domains.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: relation abstractness; number of relations combined; surface similarity of distractors; picture vs printed-word stimuli; adding a second relational dimension.
adaptive.notes: AIG from a relation-typed pair bank; distractors auto-built as surface-match, relation-reversal, and associate lures.

engagement_hook: Build a glowing bridge between pictures: each correct pair snaps a plank into place and a character walks across; wrong planks wobble, right ones lock.
construct_irrelevant_risks: This is the near-language-free verbal option, so it is the anchor against language bias; residual risks are relation familiarity carrying culture (mitigated by universal relations and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST), surface-feature capture in young children (mitigated by the warm-up + arrow scaffold), reading load only in the 6-8 word mode (mitigated by frequency leveling + an audio option), and single-tap motor keeping motor noise low.

name: Club or Odd One
one_liner: Find the picture or word that belongs with a group, or tap the one that does not fit.
interaction: Three stimuli that share a hidden property sit in a club; four candidates appear below. In Belongs mode the child taps the candidate that joins the club; in Odd-One mode four items show and the child taps the one to eject. The choice animates in/out and locks. Audio names the items for pre-readers; older bands use frequency-controlled words.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): three fruits glow together, the hand taps the fourth fruit (it flies into the club) and pushes a shoe away. One unscored warm-up (three animals + one car) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Category membership is graded around prototypes, so measuring how a child groups items reveals concept formation independent of decoding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Groups are built around clear taxonomic categories for young bands and thematic/abstract categories for older, with member typicality controlled.
learning_science.source: Rosch, E. (1975). Cognitive representations of semantic categories. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 104(3), 192-233.

learning_science.why: Choosing the odd item requires inducing the shared rule and testing candidates against it, which is core inductive reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log which candidates are sampled/hovered (M-EXPLORE) to distinguish systematic from random rule search.
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

learning_science.why: Removing written instructions keeps limited working memory on the category rule, not on decoding the task.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The club metaphor and animation teach the response with no instruction text.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257-285.

tail_precision_rationale: Distractors are built as competing-category lures (an item that fits a different but plausible rule). At the tail, choosing the target over a strong competing-category lure shows the child found the more specific/abstract shared rule; M-LURETYPE plus M-EXPLORE reveal whether high performers converge quickly on the correct rule while others sample widely, adding process resolution beyond accuracy at the cut.
age_rationale: Picture classification by taxonomic category is solvable at K-1; abstraction (function, thematic, superordinate) and printed-word items raise it to 6-8. A single tap throughout keeps motor demands flat.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete taxonomic categories -> abstract/superordinate and cross-domain word classes.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: category abstractness (perceptual -> taxonomic -> functional/abstract); member typicality; strength of the competing-category lure; picture vs word.
adaptive.notes: AIG from category-tagged banks; lures auto-selected from a sibling category to control near-miss meaning.

engagement_hook: A club-bouncer game: wave the right member in and bounce the impostor out; combos reward fast-correct choices without false ejections.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Category knowledge can reflect exposure/culture (mitigated by universal categories for young bands and adaptive drop of low-fit items via M-CONSIST); picture ambiguity (prototypical art); reading only in word mode at older bands (frequency-controlled list per the qbank); single-tap motor.

name: Spot the Silly
one_liner: Find what is silly or impossible in a picture or short story, and for older kids show why.
interaction: A scene or short scenario is presented (audio + picture for young; text for older). The child taps the impossible element (a fish riding a bike) and it highlights. For 4-5 and 6-8 a second step asks why it is silly, answered by picture/choice (young) or a short typed reason (oldest), scored for the identified violation as partial credit.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a scene shows the sun wearing mittens; the hand taps the mittens and a giggle pop appears. One unscored warm-up (an upside-down umbrella catching rain) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Detecting an impossibility requires integrating each element against world knowledge; the speed and success of that integration index verbal reasoning and knowledge structure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items embed a single well-defined world-knowledge violation and the response is tapping the violating element, separating detection from expressive language.
learning_science.source: Kutas, M., & Hillyard, S. A. (1980). Reading senseless sentences: Brain potentials reflect semantic incongruity. Science, 207(4427), 203-205.

learning_science.why: Verbal Absurdities is a long-validated marker of verbal comprehension and reasoning in standardized batteries.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep the classic construct but replace spoken-explanation scoring with taps plus an optional short justification to reduce expressive-language load for young and ELL children.
learning_science.source: Roid, G. H. (2003). Stanford-Binet Intelligence Scales, Fifth Edition (SB5): Technical Manual. Riverside.

learning_science.why: Explaining why something is impossible requires building and checking a coherent mental model of the scenario, which is the deep-comprehension signal for the why step.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The why step is scored by inference depth (M-INFDEPTH), from naming the violation to explaining its consequence.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Inference depth level reached
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: Comprehension discrimination at the tail is about inference layer, not literal recall; recording the deepest layer answered correctly (literal -> local/bridging inference -> global/thematic -> author's-purpose/evaluative) cleanly separates strong comprehenders who reach evaluative inference from those who plateau at literal.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Tag each comprehension/absurdity/cloze probe with an inference-depth level; record the maximum level answered correctly at criterion within a passage/unit.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=4-6 probes spanning depth levels per passage/unit; several passages to stabilize the estimate.

tail_precision_rationale: The two-step design turns one item into a graded measure: detecting the anomaly (M-ACC) plus articulating the correct violation and its consequence (M-POLY, M-INFDEPTH). At the tail, gifted children not only spot subtle, plausibility-graded absurdities fast (M-RTFIRST) but explain the causal/logical reason, so inference-depth scoring separates saw it from understood why precisely where the cut sits.
age_rationale: Tap-the-silly picture works at K-1 (recognition only). The explanation step and text scenarios are added at 4-5 and deepened at 6-8; the pre-reader version needs no reading or expressive language.

adaptive.content_range: Obvious visual impossibilities -> subtle plausibility violations and multi-clause scenario absurdities.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: salience of the violation; number of plausible-but-fine elements (distractor density); picture -> audio -> text; required explanation depth.
adaptive.notes: Scene templates with a swappable violation slot; explanation rubric anchors define the partial-credit categories.

engagement_hook: A silly-detector meter that giggles and fills up when you catch the impossible thing; subtler absurdities are worth more giggles.
construct_irrelevant_risks: The why step adds expressive-language/writing load (mitigated by picture/choice justification for young bands, optional speech-to-text, and keeping typed reasons out of young bands); world knowledge can be cultural (mitigated by universal physical/biological violations); single-tap motor for detection.

name: Flip It
one_liner: Find the opposite, or the closest match, of a spoken or printed word.
interaction: A target is given (audio + picture for young; printed word for older). In Opposite mode the child taps the picture/word that means the reverse; in Match mode taps the closest-in-meaning option. The choice locks with a flip animation. A frequency staircase adjusts word rarity after each answer.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a big elephant target shows; the hand taps the tiny mouse and a flip animation plays (big <-> small). One unscored warm-up (up/down arrows) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Judging antonymy/synonymy is comparing shared versus contrasting semantic features, probing depth of lexical-semantic representation beyond merely knowing a word.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Opposites use a single contrasting dimension for young items (size, height) and multi-feature contrasts for older; synonyms control shared-feature distance.
learning_science.source: Smith, E. E., Shoben, E. J., & Rips, L. J. (1974). Structure and process in semantic memory. Psychological Review, 81(3), 214-241.

learning_science.principle: Vocabulary as a reasoning/exposure proxy (Matthew effect)
learning_science.why: Depth and breadth of word-meaning relations predict verbal reasoning, but raw exposure must not be rewarded on its own.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Frequency-matched distractors and adaptive rarity ensure the score reflects semantic-relation reasoning (M-VOCABLVL) rather than simply having met the word.
learning_science.source: Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading. Reading Research Quarterly, 21(4), 360-407.

learning_science.why: Picture-opposite items let pre-readers show antonym reasoning without any print, verifying meaning across verbal and visual codes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio prompt + picture choices; printed words appear only from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Antonym/synonym items with frequency-matched lures push discrimination into fine semantic space; the adaptive rarity staircase locates the lexical ceiling (M-VOCABLVL) while lure analysis (M-LURETYPE) flags whether ceiling errors are near-synonym confusions (fine-grained, latent ability) versus associative captures, sharpening placement right at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: Concrete picture opposites (big/small, up/down, happy/sad) are within K-1 grasp with audio; abstract antonyms and nuanced synonyms with printed words extend to 6-8. Single tap; reading load only in the older word mode.

adaptive.content_range: Concrete perceptual opposites -> abstract antonyms and nuanced synonyms.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: word frequency; abstractness; opposite vs synonym mode; semantic distance of the lure; picture vs word.
adaptive.notes: Antonym/synonym pair bank tagged by frequency and semantic distance; parallel clones swap same-band pairs.

engagement_hook: A mirror world where tapping the opposite flips the scene (day -> night); Match mode magnetizes twins together.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Opposition/synonymy is highly language- and culture-loaded (the highest-bias verbal skill; mitigated by audio and picture mode for young, frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral concepts); abstract relations are hard to depict (older bands use words); single-tap motor; guessing controlled via M-CONSIST parallel items.

name: Do What I Say
one_liner: Listen to a spoken instruction and tap the picture(s) that satisfy every condition.
interaction: A grid of pictures/shapes (varying size, color, position) is shown. Audio gives a multi-condition direction (tap the small blue star that is above the tree). The child taps the matching cell(s); multi-step directions require an ordered sequence of taps; a replay button repeats the audio once. Taps lock on submit.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): audio plays the big red circle; the hand hovers each shape then taps the big red circle. One unscored warm-up (tap the yellow sun) runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Comprehending increasingly complex spoken directions (embedded clauses, multiple constraints) is a validated index of receptive language and verbal working memory.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Directions scale from one attribute to multiple embedded spatial/relational constraints acting on a controlled picture grid.
learning_science.source: De Renzi, E., & Vignolo, L. A. (1962). The Token Test: A sensitive test to detect receptive disturbances in aphasics. Brain, 85(4), 665-678.

learning_science.why: Holding several conditions while scanning taxes updating; the maximum conditions integrated is a strong reasoning- and EF-linked signal.
learning_science.concrete_decision: An adaptive condition-count staircase yields an oral-direction span (M-ORALSPAN).
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. (1992). Working memory. Science, 255(5044), 556-559.

learning_science.why: A spoken direction paired with a visual grid lets the child map language onto objects without any reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: All directions are audio; all targets are pictures/shapes on the grid.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Oral-direction condition span
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The maximum number of simultaneous spoken conditions a child can integrate before dropping one is a sharp, near-language-neutral tail separator that jointly loads receptive language and verbal working memory; gifted children reliably cross-reference 4-5 embedded constraints.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Adaptive condition-count staircase on following-oral-directions items; record the highest condition count satisfied on all constraints at criterion; log which single condition is dropped on near-misses.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: >=12-16 adaptive direction items across condition counts; report span plus the near-miss condition-drop pattern.

tail_precision_rationale: The adaptive condition-count staircase drives each child to the maximum number of simultaneous spoken constraints they can integrate (M-ORALSPAN / M-DIFFREACH), a sharp tail separator because gifted children hold and cross-reference 4-5 embedded conditions where others drop one. The tap sequence (M-PATH) shows whether they resolve constraints systematically, and near-misses (one condition dropped) are logged distinctly for fine placement.
age_rationale: One- or two-condition directions with pictures work at K-1; embedded-clause, multi-step directions extend to 6-8. No reading is required at any band (audio); motor is a tap or short tap sequence.

adaptive.content_range: Single attribute -> multiple embedded spatial/relational/conditional constraints and multi-step sequences.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: number of conditions; embedding/relational complexity; grid size; sequence length; single vs multi-tap; one replay allowed.
adaptive.notes: A grammar-templated direction generator over an attribute-tagged grid; auto-scored against the constraint set.

engagement_hook: A spell-caster vibe: each correct multi-condition tap casts a glowing rune, and longer instructions unlock bigger spells; it feels like Simon Says with magic.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Loads verbal working memory and can confound with pure reasoning (reported alongside WM; a single replay caps memory-only failure); audio clarity (caption fallback in the demo; production audio + replay); grid scanning adds visual-search/processing-speed variance (mitigated by untimed taps and modest grid sizes); language background (dialect-neutral, frequency-leveled direction wording).

name: Story Quest
one_liner: Follow a short story (listened to or read) and answer questions that require inferring who, why, and what happens next.
interaction: An illustrated narrative plays in segments (audio + picture for young; text passage for older). At pause points a probe appears with picture or text choices (who wanted what / why / what next / fact vs opinion); older bands add one short writing-to-sources constructed response scored by rubric as partial credit. Answers lock and the story continues.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): a two-panel scene plays (a child reaches for a cookie jar), a probe shows two faces (happy/sad); the hand taps the fitting face and the story continues. One unscored warm-up probe runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Deep comprehension is building a coherent mental model, not recalling words; inference probes at pause points measure model quality directly.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes target the situation model (goals, causes, predictions) rather than verbatim recall; distractors match surface text to catch shallow readers.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review, 95(2), 163-182.

learning_science.why: Drawing local and global inferences distinguishes strong comprehenders beyond word reading.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes are graded from literal -> local inference -> global/thematic -> author's-purpose/evaluative (M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Cain, K., & Oakhill, J. (1999). Inference making ability and its relation to comprehension failure. Reading and Writing, 11(5), 489-503.

learning_science.why: Embedding probes inside an engaging narrative reduces the test anxiety and disengagement that bias comprehension scores.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes are woven into the quest with process logging (progress, persistence, hints) under an ECD evidence model.
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J. (2011). Stealth assessment in computer-based games to support learning. In Computer Games and Instruction (pp. 503-524). Information Age Publishing.

tail_precision_rationale: Comprehension tail signal comes from inference depth, not literal recall: M-INFDEPTH records the deepest layer (up to author's-purpose/evaluative) a child answers correctly, and M-POLY grades the constructed writing-to-sources response. Because probes escalate within one passage, a single unit yields a curve (M-PROG) that distinguishes readers who sustain deep inference from those who plateau at literal, exactly the discrimination needed at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: Listening comprehension with picture answers makes this valid at K-1 (no reading); the identical probe engine switches to read passages and constructed responses at 4-5 and 6-8. Constructed responses (writing load) are reserved for 6-8.

adaptive.content_range: Simple narrative with literal/one-step inference (young) -> multi-paragraph literary/informational text with global inference, fact/opinion, and author's purpose (6-8).
adaptive.difficulty_levers: passage length/complexity; required inference depth; listening vs reading; MCQ vs constructed; surface-match strength of distractors.
adaptive.notes: Quality passages are hard to fully auto-generate; probe sets and distractors are templatable over a human-curated passage bank.

engagement_hook: A branching quest where correct inferences unlock the next scene and collect story-gems; the child is a character advancing the plot, not taking a reading test.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Reading decoding can confound comprehension at older bands (mitigated by a listening mode and by separating decoding from inference via picture probes for young bands); constructed responses add writing load (6-8 only; rubric scores the idea not mechanics; optional speech-to-text); background knowledge (balanced topics and novel worlds); engagement gated by M-ENGAGE/M-PERSIST.

name: Fill the Gap
one_liner: Complete a sentence with the missing idea by picking the picture or word that best fills the gap.
interaction: A sentence is presented with a blank (audio with a beep at the gap plus pictures for young; a printed sentence with a blank plus word choices for older). The child taps the best option; it drops into the blank and the full sentence plays/reads back. Context-clue items require using the rest of the sentence; a scrambled-tiles variant asks the child to drag words into a meaningful order.
self_teach: Ghost-hand demo (<10s): the dog wants to ___ plays with pictures (bone / car / cloud); the hand taps the bone, it slots into the blank, and the sentence replays. One unscored warm-up runs before scoring.

learning_science.why: Filling a deleted element measures integration of syntactic and semantic context, a validated comprehension and language-proficiency index.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Gaps are placed so only contextual reasoning (not a single collocation) selects the answer; distractors fit locally but not globally.
learning_science.source: Taylor, W. L. (1953). Cloze procedure: A new tool for measuring readability. Journalism Quarterly, 30(4), 415-433.

learning_science.why: Using surrounding context to infer the right word is a hallmark of strong verbal reasoning and predicts vocabulary growth.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Higher bands include low-frequency target words recoverable only from context (M-VOCABLVL + M-INFDEPTH).
learning_science.source: Sternberg, R. J. (1987). Most vocabulary is learned from context. In M. G. McKeown & M. E. Curtis (Eds.), The Nature of Vocabulary Acquisition (pp. 89-105). Erlbaum.

learning_science.why: Oral sentence + picture completion lets pre-readers show sentence reasoning with no print.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Young items are audio sentence frames with picture options; printed cloze appears only from 4-5 up.
learning_science.source: Paivio, A. (1986). Mental Representations: A Dual Coding Approach. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: Context-recoverable low-frequency targets make this a joint vocabulary-by-inference tail probe: M-VOCABLVL captures the rarity of words a child can pin from context and M-INFDEPTH captures whether they used global sentence meaning versus a local collocation. Parallel matched gaps (M-CONSIST) tighten the standard error right at the cut, and first-action latency (M-RTFIRST) flags reflective integration over guess-and-check.
age_rationale: Oral sentence completion with picture answers is valid at K-1 (no reading); printed cloze with context clues extends to 6-8. Single tap; reading load only in the older printed mode, offset by an audio option.

adaptive.content_range: Simple oral sentence + picture completion -> multi-clause cloze requiring global context and rare target words; a scrambled-order variant covers sentence arrangement.
adaptive.difficulty_levers: context distance (local vs whole-sentence); target word frequency; syntactic complexity; picture vs word; number of options.
adaptive.notes: Sentence-frame bank with gap slots; distractors auto-tagged local-fit vs global-fit; the scrambled-order variant supports sentence_arrangement.

engagement_hook: A missing-puzzle-piece snap: the right piece clicks into the sentence and the scene it describes comes alive (the dog actually chews the bone).
construct_irrelevant_risks: Sentence completion is language- and exposure-loaded (mitigated by audio for young bands, frequency leveling, and ELL-neutral frames); local-collocation shortcuts (mitigated by global-fit-only gaps with local-fit lures); reading load at older bands (audio option); single-tap motor.

name: Firefly Trail (spatial span)
one_liner: Fireflies (tiles) light up one-by-one in a growing sequence and the child taps them back in the same order, or in reverse.
interaction: N tiles in a 3x3 grid flash sequentially; the child reproduces the sequence by tapping tiles, and a Backward toggle asks for reverse order. Re-tapping a selected tile de-selects it (logged as a revision). The trial auto-submits at N taps; span rises by 1 after a correct trial and drops by 1 after an error (Levitt 1-up/1-down staircase).
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand watches three tiles flash then taps them in order and shows a check mark (about 6s), followed by one unscored warm-up trial; no text is required.

learning_science.why: A standardized, language-free index of visuospatial short-term memory that dissociates from verbal span.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a 3x3 tile grid with sequential lighting and same-order tap-back as the core mechanic.
learning_science.source: Kessels, R. P. C., van Zandvoort, M. J. E., Postma, A., Kappelle, L. J., & de Haan, E. H. F. (2000). The Corsi Block-Tapping Task: standardization and normative data. Applied Neuropsychology, 7(4), 252-258.

learning_science.principle: Capacity limit of about four chunks
learning_science.why: Working-memory capacity centers near 3-5 items, so a staircase around this range maximizes information at the tail.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Start span at 3 and adapt by plus/minus 1; extend the item bank to spans 8-9 for above-level probing.
learning_science.source: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87-114.

learning_science.why: Backward reproduction adds central-executive manipulation beyond passive storage.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Offer a Backward mode and report the forward-minus-backward manipulation cost.
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), The Psychology of Learning and Motivation (Vol. 8, pp. 47-89). Academic Press.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Memory span threshold
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The staircase-estimated longest sequence a child reliably reproduces is a continuous, fine-grained capacity index that keeps separating high performers who all hit ceiling on fixed-length items.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Track the highest sequence length reproduced correctly under a 1-up/1-down span staircase; average the last several reversal lengths.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: 6-10 adaptive trials per mode (forward/backward) for a stable threshold.

new_measurements_proposed.name: Manipulation cost
new_measurements_proposed.usefulness_tail: The drop from forward (storage) span to backward/reorder (manipulation) span isolates central-executive manipulation, which tracks fluid reasoning better than raw storage at the tail.
new_measurements_proposed.how_to_collect: Compute forward max span minus backward or sorted max span under matched staircases.
new_measurements_proposed.how_much_to_collect: Enough trials in each mode to estimate both spans (6-10 each).

tail_precision_rationale: Reproduction accuracy is dichotomous and saturates fast among gifted children, so this type extracts tail signal from process: the staircase-estimated span threshold (M-SPAN) and max reached (M-DIFFREACH) give a continuous capacity index above grade level, forward-minus-backward manipulation cost (M-MANIPCOST) isolates executive manipulation from passive storage, and consistency measures (M-RTVAR, M-LAPSE) plus order-vs-item error typing (M-ERRTYPE) separate secure high-capacity solvers from lucky ones by scoring on lapses rather than raw speed.
age_rationale: Wordless, tap-only and language-free, so it runs from K-1 (framed as catching fireflies, spans 2-3) upward; older bands unlock the Backward mode and spans of 6-9. Targets are large (66px) to remove fine-motor demands for little hands; only tapping (no drag) is required.

adaptive.content_range: K-1 short forward spans (2-3) with animal framing up to 6-8 backward spans of 8-9 and denser grids
adaptive.difficulty_levers: sequence length, forward vs backward, presentation rate, grid size, optional delayed spatial-recognition array variant
adaptive.notes: Span is a native psychophysical staircase and sequences are procedurally generated, so unlimited matched clones exist for M-CONSIST parallel forms.

engagement_hook: A glowing firefly trail that visibly grows each time you succeed, so leveling up feels like lighting a longer and longer path.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motor: tap accuracy on small or close tiles (mitigated by large targets, tap-not-drag). Familiarity: Simon-style novelty (mitigated by ghost-hand plus warm-up). Attention/ADHD: sustained attention and impulsivity can depress span and inflate variability, mimicking low capacity; flag by gating on M-ENGAGE/M-DRIFT and treating occasional lapses as process signal rather than capacity, requiring consistency across trials before a tail decision. Device: touch vs mouse latency and screen size affect tile spacing.

name: Critter Line-Up (list sorting / digit span)
one_liner: Critters (or numbers) parade by one at a time, then the child lines them up in a required order - same, reversed, or sorted by size - by tapping them into slots.
interaction: A sequence of N items is shown one-by-one on a belt; the child then fills N ordered slots by tapping items from a shuffled tray. A rule toggle sets the target order to repeat, reverse, or sort (by real-life size for animals, ascending for numbers). Tapping a filled slot returns the item to the tray (revision). It auto-submits when all slots are filled; list length adapts plus/minus 1.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches three animals then taps them smallest-to-biggest into the slots with a check mark (about 6s); one unscored warm-up follows. Size is depicted concretely (ant to whale) so sorting needs no reading.

learning_science.principle: List Sorting working memory (storage plus manipulation)
learning_science.why: Requiring items to be reordered by a dimension taps the central executive, not just storage, and is validated in the NIH Toolbox child battery.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use a name-then-reorder-by-size mechanic with animals for young children and numbers for older ones.
learning_science.source: Tulsky, D. S., Carlozzi, N., Chiaravalloti, N. D., et al. (2014). NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery: List Sorting Working Memory subtest. Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society, 20(6), 599-610.

learning_science.principle: Phonological loop and central executive (Baddeley model)
learning_science.why: Forward span indexes the phonological/storage buffer while reorder and reverse tap central-executive manipulation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Provide repeat, reverse and sort rules and report the manipulation cost across them.
learning_science.source: Baddeley, A. (2000). The episodic buffer: a new component of working memory? Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4(11), 417-423.

learning_science.why: Higher-ability children impose structure (grouping, rehearsal) that shows up in serial-position and error patterns.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score partial credit by position and log intrusion vs novel errors to reveal strategy.
learning_science.source: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two: some limits on our capacity for processing information. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81-97.
